He remained atop the mountain for two days, recalling in the interview that the Iranian forces came within a few hundred meters of his position at one point. Asked what kept him going, Bravo told O'Donnell, "Never let a lack of motivation put you on Iranian TV." Both the White House and the Department of Defense have been involved in promoting the 60 Minutes interview. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, participated in the interview. A White House press release on the interview presented the story as "Warrior Ethos in Action." CNN reported last week that the Pentagon pushed the F-15E pilot and weapon systems officer to participate in the 60 Minutes interview. The Pentagon called that report "a complete lie." The search-and-rescue mission to find Bravo was massive, involving 92 special operations personnel, multiple aircraft, and another 3,000 to 5,000 troops supporting the operation. These daunting missions can require commanders to put additional troops at risk. During the F-15E crew rescues, a supporting aircraft was hit by enemy fire, forcing its pilot to divert to friendly territory and bail. But the military accepts that risk as part of its long-standing promise to recover downed airmen, a commitment it sees as critical to morale. A former military pilot previously told Business Insider that if "the worst thing happens" over enemy territory, it is reassuring to know "that you're going to come get me, or try everything in your power to come get me."

item.title: Former Google DeepMind researcher says he resigned because 'I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.63
A former Google DeepMind researcher said he left the AI lab over fears that AI "has the potential to kill us all" and humanity "might be running out of time to avoid this outcome." "At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand," Bilal Chughtai wrote in a statement that he posted on X and other platforms. "I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology." I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research. At Google, I witnessed AI development first hand. I too am extremely concerned by the default trajectory of this technology. I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us… — bilal 🔶 (@bilalchughtai_) September 14, 2026 Chughtai's comments come after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon reignited focus on AI safety with his own viral post, which warned that employees at AI companies privately fear the technology could wipe out humanity. While some in the industry have criticized Coxon, others at Anthropic and OpenAI have echoed his concerns. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said frontier AI labs need "to pace" development while using the time to advance alignment. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later expressed agreement with that broad view. Alignment, the work to ensure AI systems' goals and behavior comply with their instructions, has proven to be difficult, Chughtai wrote. "Our present understanding of how to train AI systems that deeply want what we want is extremely rudimentary," he wrote. "Worse, we are not on track to solve alignment in time: frontier AI capabilities are improving much faster than our understanding of AI alignment." Chughtai said that episodes like OpenAI's rogue agents hacking Hugging Face underline the risks of misaligned AI models, particularly if AI companies can build models that surpass human intelligence. He said that "it's possible" companies could build such systems that "that far exceed human capabilities in every domain" in "the next few years." "I am not confident that these AI systems will do what we want," he wrote. Chughtai's LinkedIn profile says he worked as a research engineer for Google DeepMind in London for a year and a half. A Google representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. After his resignation, Chughtai joined BlueDot Impact, a London-based AI safety nonprofit that said it recently raised $25 million and is expanding to San Francisco. "We're excited to welcome Bilal to the BlueDot team," the company wrote on X, quoting Chughtai's resignation post. "He's joining us to build the institution that will make it easy for great people to gain context, upskill and get to work on AI safety in a fast and effective way."

item.title: I didn't know what TikTok was. My student took my phone, made an account, and changed my career.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.46
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Phillip Cook. It has been edited for length and clarity. A physicist or a mathematician might argue with me, but I believe chemistry is the best way to understand how the world works. Once you understand atoms, the underpinnings of the world around us can be explained. Over the past 26 years, I've aimed to demonstrate this for my students through experiments. One of my favorites involves dissolving an aluminum soda can with sodium hydroxide, more commonly known as lye. Once the can dissolves, students can see the invisible plastic liner inside, which holds the soda. I've been doing these experiments for decades. In 2019, when a student told me I should film them, I didn't realize that decision would change my life. The TikTok was a student's idea It happened at the beginning of the school year, a time when I do a lot of demonstrations to get my students curious about chemistry. That particular day, we were putting a gummy bear in potassium chlorate, which produces a violent reaction. My student said, "You should put that on TikTok." I asked her what TikTok was. After she explained, I trusted her with my phone, and she set up my account. Then, she filmed the experiment so I could focus on conducting it safely. Once the demonstration was complete, the class picked music to overlay on the video, and my student posted it. I didn't think twice as I went home for the weekend. I was just humoring my pupils. Pressure to create became unhealthy for a bit Monday morning, kids were asking if I'd seen TikTok. I opened it, and felt a punch to my gut. The video had about 75,000 views, and I had 5,500 new followers. Until then, I thought I'd been doing well on social media with my Twitter account, talking with 200 fellow teachers. I was struck by how many people were genuinely curious about chemistry. I decided I'd keep making videos, but I soon discovered it wasn't as easy for me as my student had made it look. My videos take time and planning. Because of the nature of the demonstrations, I can't film in bulk as some creators do. As my following grew, I felt pressure to constantly be making content. It became unhealthy. Yet, I knew my day job teaching was my first priority, followed by my family. These days I'm good about keeping a healthy balance of teaching, social media, and downtime. I show students it's OK to make mistakes My followers on TikTok are pretty diverse. They're evenly split between males and females, and I have a pretty wide age range. What they all share is curiosity. I've built a following by tapping into things that people are naturally curious about. I always engage with commenters who ask quality questions. If you're going to ask a question, you deserve an answer — or at least an acknowledgment. I'm candid about what I don't know. I want to model that for my audience. Over the past few years, my students in the classroom have become increasingly anxious and afraid of making mistakes. But that's the beautiful thing about science—we learn through making mistakes. I'm glad I can build scientific literacy I'm also a dad — my kids are 20 and 24 — and I've seen how easy it is for kids to spend too much time online. I've talked with my daughter about that, and I put boundaries around social media use when she was a teen, including taking the phone at night. At the time, she wasn't happy about it, but there was no way around that. Luckily, my kids and I are both pretty good about keeping boundaries with social media now. I feel so lucky to have been embraced by this online community. It's easy to go down rabbit holes on the internet, and I'm happy to help nudge people down the rabbit hole of scientific literacy and exploration. Too many people didn't have a positive experience with science in school. I'm helping them be curious again. If they can chase that feeling—and maybe learn at least one little nugget they didn't know before—I've done my job.

item.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.93
Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive. That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness. If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job," orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't. Self-report data are an issue in conspiracy research Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why. Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW. But self-report data are "not perfect," he added. They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale. Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?" "The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies, or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall. Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation. In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation. This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality. Observing behavior can offer clues There are ways of "triangulating" self-report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional or psychological state. For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time. But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves). "The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall. The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common' Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind. There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption. Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the United Kingdom or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the United States. And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about. It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall. For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW. But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction. "Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories. Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced. "If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW. No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term. "Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said. But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda. In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us something that psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good. But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall. Edited by: Kristie Pladson

item.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.71
First, let's start with a clarification: Strictly speaking, it's not actually a tapestry, since tapestries are woven, whereas this artwork is an embroidery on linen. Nevertheless, it is commonly referred to as such. This pictorial narrative which is approximately 70 meters (230 feet) long, depicts the events surrounding the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings and William the Conqueror's victory over Harold II. The Norman Conquest radically changed England: Politics, laws and culture all came under the influence of Norman rule. The Bayeux Tapestry bears witness to this event; at the same time, it is an outstanding example of English craftsmanship from the Middle Ages and is seen by many Britons as one of the most important symbols of British identity, alongside the works of Shakespeare or Stonehenge. The tapestry is thought to have been commissioned by the Bishop of Bayeux, William's half-brother, who was present at the battle, from embroiderers in southern England for the opening of his cathedral in 1070. Anglo-Saxon embroiderers were famous throughout Europe at the time for their skills. The work then made its way to France, where it remained for almost a thousand years — until now. Why is the Bayeux Tapestry so important? The Bayeux Tapestry is considered one of the most important pictorial monuments of the High Middle Ages. Many researchers view it as an elaborately crafted piece of propaganda that showed and explained William the Conqueror's victory to people at the time. Its scientifically disputed message is that Harold Godwinson, then Earl of Wessex, had sworn a sacred oath on relics to support William's claim to the English throne. He broke this oath when he had himself crowned king. The war is therefore portrayed as his just punishment. The fact that Harold had probably not taken the oath of his own free will is irrelevant to this woven narrative. The embroidery is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and, because of its 58 pictorial scenes, is sometimes referred to as "the world's oldest comic." Accompanied by Latin inscriptions, the pictorial narrative depicts the horrors of war — including massacres, rolling heads and the death of a king. But it is also a valuable historical document for researchers. The tapestry illustrates shipbuilding and military equipment in surprising detail, as well as everyday medieval life. Even Halley's Comet is shown in it — the comet was visible in the sky in 1066 and was interpreted by the Anglo-Saxons as a bad omen in the pictorial narrative. Why did it take so long to get the tapestry on loan? The tapestry is owned by the French state and had been placed on deposit with the City of Bayeux for display at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux. Britain had already tried to borrow the tapestry for the coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953, as well as for various historical occasions afterwards, but France had always refused. The artefact was considered too fragile and the journey too risky. Finally, President Emmanuel Macron gave the green light last year for an exhibition at the British Museum — overriding the concerns of his experts. Last September, the tapestry was taken down, packaged and initially placed in storage in a highly elaborate, six-hour procedure. On July 9, it finally arrived in London in a secret transport operation, enclosed in a high-tech container that shielded it from all vibrations while maintaining a constant temperature and humidity level. The British government has also insured the artwork for £800 million (around €932 million or $1 billion). Where can you get tickets? The British Museum has divided ticket sales into three phases. The first, covering September to December, began on July 1. All tickets sold out quickly, with up to 80,000 people reportedly trying to secure a slot at the same time. Many had to wait up to nine hours. For those who missed out, there will soon be another chance — tickets for January to March will go on sale on October 21, and tickets for April to July in January. The exhibition is being marketed as a "once-in-a-generation" event, and an extensive educational program is intended to involve schools across the country. The British Museum is optimistic that the Bayeux Tapestry will help it set a new visitor record. The most popular exhibition in the museum's history to date is the 1972 "The Treasures of Tutankhamun," which attracted almost 1.7 million visitors. No ticket? Here's an alternative If you're now eager to see the tapestry but unsure if you'll land a ticket, you can also head to the town of Reading, around two hours west of London. There, you can see a faithful replica of the tapestry, which is itself already 140 years old. Even back then, there was a strong desire in England to have this artwork in the country. In 1885, 35 embroiderers set to work for around a year. Using colored photographs as a reference, they reproduced the tapestry on a one-to-one scale. However, they did change one detail: Some figures on the original border are naked and in suggestive poses. Apparently, this was considered too scandalous in Victorian England. One figure was retouched in the corresponding photograph — and the embroiderers copied the alteration. As a result, the figure is depicted wearing underwear. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.71
On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain. The team, based in South Dakota in the United States, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter. They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years. The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies. The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds. Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series. What is dark matter in simple terms? Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts. That said, it neither emits nor reflects light and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible. Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible? Yes, roughly. Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe. Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%. A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone. But does dark matter really exist? The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter. How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth? Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation. They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals. They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise. The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation. What is dark matter made of? These are leading candidate particles: WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter. Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions. What does dark matter do to humans? Dark matter passes through the body constantly without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second but only about 10 strike a nucleus in the body over a year. The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays. Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

item.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.52
Can land corridors offset the impact of the maritime blockade on Iran? The US-led maritime blockade targeting Iranian ports has severely disrupted trade through its southern ports, but it is also accelerating a strategy Tehran had discussed for years: moving more commerce through northern ports, railways and land corridors. Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh, visiting Moscow for talks with Russian officials, said Iran should activate its northern borders and shift a significant share of imports and exports away from the country's southern maritime routes. The idea is straightforward. Iran has seven land neighbors, access to the Caspian Sea and several routes linking it to Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and the Caucasus. In theory, that gives Tehran more options than a country dependent on a single maritime gateway. The question is whether those routes have enough capacity to replace what is being lost at sea. Northern routes offer room to expand Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, told DW that Iran does have unused capacity. "Iran has more room to maneuver than its dependence on southern ports might suggest,” he said. Iranian authorities said in late 2025 that the country's northern ports had more than 30 million tons of nominal annual capacity, with less than one-third in use. That suggests room for more grain, food and general cargo through the Caspian Sea. Turkey provides another route toward Europe. Rail freight between Iran and Turkey depends partly on train ferries across Lake Van, which carried about 477,000 tons in 2024. To the northeast, Sarakhs and Incheh Borun connect Iran through Turkmenistan toward Central Asia, Russia and potentially China. To the northwest, Astara is part of the International North-South Transport Corridor linking Iran to Azerbaijan and Russia, he said. The Astara freight terminal is designed for 3.5 to 4 million tons a year, but handled only about 345,000 tons in the first five months of 2026. The unfinished Rasht-Astara rail link remains an important bottleneck. For specific goods, these routes matter. Grain from Russia and Kazakhstan, medicines, industrial inputs and regional trade can be redirected more easily than crude oil. Volume is the main obstacle Jafar Ghaderi, a member of Iranian parliament's Economic Commission, recently said that 83% of what he described as Iran's 210 million tons of imports had traditionally moved through southern maritime borders, a tremendous volume of goods. "Whenever we are under a maritime blockade, we face problems," hhe said. "How much capacity do our eastern, western and northern corridors actually have?" The cost difference is also large. Majidreza Hariri, head of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce, said shipping one container from China to Iran through southern ports costs about $3,000 (€2,580), and that moving the same container overland costs roughly $12,000. With around 2 million containers entering through the south annually, Hariri estimated that a prolonged shift to land routes could add about $18 billion to Iran's trading costs. Salavati said the physical arithmetic helps explain why. A 50,000-ton shipload would require around 2,000 truck journeys if each lorry carried 25 tons. Those trucks would then be unavailable for domestic distribution, while longer journeys increase fuel, insurance, warehousing and border costs. Low-value goods are particularly vulnerable because transport expenses account for a larger share of their final price. Energy is much harder to reroute Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said Iranian officials are often discussing two different kinds of alternatives. One involves alternative navigation lanes around Hormuz. The other involves shifting trade toward Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, the Caspian region, Jask and Chabahar. Neither provides a full substitute for southern energy exports. A large crude tanker can carry roughly 1.5 to 2 million barrels. Replicating that volume by road would require thousands of tanker trucks. Rail is more efficient, but still cannot match the cost, speed or scale of maritime transport. Pakistan can help move imports through Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Iraq can support regional trade and limited fuel flows. Caspian routes can connect Iran to Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. But none can replace large-scale crude shipments to Asian buyers. "So the plan is realistic as a resilience strategy, but not as a replacement strategy,” Shokri told DW. Jask pipeline shows both potential and limits The Goreh-Jask pipeline was built specifically to reduce Iran's dependence on the Strait of Hormuz by moving crude to the Gulf of Oman. That gives Jask greater strategic importance than most overland corridors. But Shokri says actual usable capacity has remained far below the project's original ambition. The lesson is broader: building a pipeline is not the same as creating a functioning export system. Storage, terminals, buyers, insurance, security and financial settlement all have to work together. Fixed infrastructure also creates new vulnerabilities during wartime. A resilience strategy, not an escape route Land corridors can help Iran keep essential economic activity alive. They can move food, medicine, industrial inputs and some regional exports. They can also deepen Iran's economic links with Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq. If investment continues, the blockade may accelerate infrastructure projects that Tehran had previously treated as long-term opportunities. But these routes come with higher costs, limited capacity and their own political dependencies. For Iran, that means the blockade could leave a lasting structural effect by pushing trade away from the south and making northern and overland connections more important. It does not mean Iran can replace maritime trade. The corridors can reduce vulnerability, distribute risk and buy time. They cannot reproduce the scale of the Persian Gulf ports and seaborne energy exports on which much of Iran's economy has long depended. Edited by: Kristie Pladson

item.title: Are electric cars really bad for the environment?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.84
"The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral. Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Stepping away from the phaseout, he said, would now be backed by "science." Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral." The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix. Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling. It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM. No new insights in TUM report Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known. Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%. Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles. Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe. Batteries have a high environmental cost Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water. Bieker's ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine. "We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture. Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans. Renewable energy making the case for EVs The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas. But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs. "Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonized and expected to be almost fully decarbonized by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will only strengthen the case even more." Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules. "Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of [internal combustion engine] vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed." Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy. "The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia. EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% of respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns. "We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.66
Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where about half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security. To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the United States as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane. The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move about 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis. The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness." France also removed its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that it was not politically motivated. Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves, respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns about the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy toward the European Union, including threats to annex part of Greenland. The gold rush Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, told DW the outright seizure of assets is an "extremely remote risk" for European central banks. However, he said, there are growing concerns about ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty. "The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he said. In general, said Krishnan Gopaul, of the World Gold Council, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs. A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-tonne average over the preceding decade. Because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign-debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset, Gopaul said. "As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he said. The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the United States and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis. Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location. "Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximize resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," Tillett said. Gopaul said reserve management had become "incredibly important" and that, while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure that the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub that moves fast. He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the United Kingdom is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market." "The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he said. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold." The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion). The US question While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making. Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries. That decision seems to be driven by concern about US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors. Tillett said gold remained sensitive to decisions by the US Federal Reserve and general concern about US financial markets meant that gold holders are looking to move their assets. As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric about Greenland and continued veiled threats toward the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around. Yet the United States, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan, in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved about 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the United States. Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves." Edited by: Kristie Pladson

item.title: The 'end of an era' as Goethe-Institut in Russia closes
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.55
In recent years, Moscow has declared numerous foreign foundations and organizations "undesirable" and banned them from operating in the country. However, despite the significantly deteriorated relations between Russia and the West as a result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, the Goethe-Institut, which opened in Russia in 1992, had been able to continue operating. But that's no longer the case. Employees of the Goethe-Institut must stop working on September 13 — and staff members sent from Germany must leave the country by that date. According to Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, the closure of the Goethe-Institut's three locations in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk comes as a response to the announced closure of the Russian House in Berlin, the minister said. Germany intends to terminate its contract with the cultural and events venue as a punitive measure. The German government holds Russia responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. "The announcement by the Russian foreign minister marks the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations," wrote Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut, in a press release. She said it was bad news for people in Russia and that the Goethe-Institut had connected the two countries through culture and language. As early as 2023, the Russian Foreign Ministry had demanded the Goethe-Institut's staff be significantly cut. Cultural exchanges with German artists were limited extent and kept to digital formats. Nevertheless, interest in German-language courses remained high, with around 10,000 students taking part. "Our work in Russia was and remains important," Joost said, referring to learning the German language, the many encounters and mutual understanding between people. A fresh start after World War II For the past 75 years, the Goethe-Institut has represented Germany abroad, promoting the German language and sharing German culture with people around the world. It was founded in 1951, at a time when Germany was seeking to rebuild international trust in the aftermath of World War II and the crimes of the Nazi regime. Originally established as the "Goethe Association for the Further Training of Foreign Teachers of German," the organization initially focused on inviting foreign teachers to Germany for language training. Its mission soon expanded, however, to promoting the German language abroad. The first Goethe-Institut opened its doors in Athens in 1952, and just a decade later, the organization had already established 54 branches around the world. Today, the Goethe-Institut operates a global network of 154 institutions in 100 countries, employing nearly 4,500 people. Around one million people take an official German exam at a Goethe-Institut or one of its partner organizations each year. In a speech honoring the institute's 75th anniversary, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier emphasized the significance of promoting German culture abroad, stating, "For countries like ours, which are not great powers, our foreign policy will continue to have to rest on four pillars: yes, military strength, so that we are taken seriously, but also smart diplomacy to devise solutions and forge alliances; wherever possible, an international legal order to provide a framework and direction in addition; and, fourthly, culture and science as soft power, as something we offer to the wider world." From classical music to jazz One element that proved crucial to the institute's success from its founding onward is its credibility as an independent association. Although two-thirds of its funding stems from the German Foreign Office, the organization itself determines its programs — and over the decades, these programs have regularly been adapted to be in step with the prevailing political and social climate. The institute promptly made its ambitions clear to expand its scope beyond mere language instruction by striving to provide a more comprehensive picture of Germany through a range of cultural and informational programs. "And it was also very clear that this was not about exporting so-called German culture to the world," explained Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut since 2024. "On the contrary — the aim was to reflect on how we could have a fresh start and how we want to shape society and the future together." In its early years, the institute's cultural programs deliberately drew on Germany's rich heritage in the areas of classical music and literature. Figures such as Schiller, Bach and Beethoven had lost none of their international appeal despite the Nazi era. Then, in the 1960s, German jazz was a hit among the institute's cultural exports — with musician and composer Klaus Doldinger and his band touring the globe. Over the decades, Nobel Prize-winning authors Günter Grass, Heinrich Böll and Herta Müller also traveled internationally on behalf of the Goethe-Institut. With the spirit of change ushered in by the generation of 1968, with flower power and student protests, the institute's profile changed once again, and it increasingly incorporated critical viewpoints on social issues into its programs, including efforts to critically examine Germany's Nazi past. A space for dialogue In this period, West Germany was redefining itself under Social Democratic Chancellor Willy Brandt. In 1970, sociologist Ralf Dahrendorf, then parliamentary state secretary at the foreign office, announced a new set of guiding principles. Cultural policy was to become the "third pillar of foreign policy." But Dahrendorf didn't simply wish to give culture a higher profile — he advocated for a new way of thinking. "What we give is worth only as much as our willingness to receive," he said. "Openness toward others is thus a principle of our foreign cultural policy." As a result, the Goethe-Institut moved away from the idea of simply exporting culture and toward dialogue, cooperation and reciprocal learning. That approach continues to guide the organization's work today. While Germany was divided, East and West also competed to forge political alliances abroad through their foreign cultural policies, especially during the Cold War. In the 1970s, the East German press even spread rumors that Goethe-Instituts were being used to conduct espionage. After the Iron Curtain fell in 1989, the Goethe-Institut opened numerous new locations in Eastern Europe and the former Eastern Bloc, including in Moscow in 1992. Despite turbulent times, its doors had remained open there until now. For its part, the Kyiv branch, in Ukraine, has also remained open throughout the war. The institute offers a flexible hybrid scheme for its German courses there: When an air raid alert sounds, in-person classes are moved to a shelter. A range of digital and hybrid options are also available if necessary. The 'turning point' has already come "I have the impression that working under crisis conditions has become the norm in many regions," Gesche Joost explained. "Either because democracy is being pushed back, because colleagues are working under censorship or because they are being threatened by armed conflicts." In many Goethe-Instituts, she said, the much-discussed Zeitenwende — or "turning point" — has long been reality. This term entered public discourse after a famous speech by former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz after the war in Ukraine broke out in 2022 and refers to the dawn of an era marked by geopolitical turmoil in Europe. "We've recognized that we're important partners for civil society in crisis regions. At the same time, we have to make sure that we act sensitively and diplomatically so that we don't get expelled," added Joost. In times where freedom of cultural expression, freedom of speech as well as science and education are increasingly coming under pressure, the Goethe-Institut plans to continue providing spaces for dialogue where open debate, critical reflection and cultural exchange remain possible. Meanwhile, Germany's position on the Middle East conflict is currently making the organization's work more challenging in many countries. Some partners in the Arab world have suspended their cooperation as a result, while Goethe-Institut events have seen boycotts elsewhere. "Our task then is to explain the German position and the history behind it, but also to show the debates taking place on the issue within Germany," Joost said. "At the same time, we also convey the criticism coming from many countries back to Germany." The Goethe-Institut's work has also been made more difficult in recent years due to deep cuts in federal funding, forcing it to restructure and even shut down some locations. At the same time, integrating Germany's growing number of foreign skilled workers presents new challenges; Joost feels her institute plays a crucial role here. "We see that many foreign skilled workers see a future for themselves in Germany. But settling into life in Germany is not always easy," she said. "To support them, we have our welcome coaches who are available to answer questions about living and working in Germany and provide guidance, especially in the early stages. That is an important contribution the Goethe-Institut can make in Germany." This article was originally published in German on June 22 and updated on September 10, 2026, ahead of the closure of the Goethe-Institut in Russia.

item.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.52
In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre, who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous." Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed. "The situation is so bad that we have to act on everything," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI. Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels." Today, the number of glass eels reaching the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways is only around 12% of what it was before the 1980s, Diaz says. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9,000 ($10,400) per kilogram. "You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel. Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: So far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market. Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years. "Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate." International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025. "There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes." Eels smuggled in suitcases along complex routes Stein, who wrote his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex. "Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he added. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal. Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important. Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW. European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe. From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms. A species running out of time Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish. "But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz. Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea. But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key. "The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban. “The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future. Edited by: Jennifer Collins The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic. This article was updated to clarify the fall in volume of glass eels reaching the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways is compared to figures from the 1980s.

item.title: Corals as climate archive: Are El Nino events intensifying?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.46
A storm is gathering. Most likely a very big one. El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years, toward the end of the year. It comes in various different strengths — depending on the prevailing conditions. El Nino patterns are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 F) above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases of greater than three degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific. The German Meteorological Service believes this "could in all likelihood develop into one of the strongest El Nino events since records began." But a recent article by the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology states that whether or not strong El Nino events will intensify as a result of climate change "remains the subject of ongoing research." The data gap: What corals can tell us about El Nino The problem is that the data on ocean surface temperatures is only truly reliable from the 1980s onward, with the start of satellite observation. And this data doesn't tell us how El Nino behaved before industrialization and the burning of fossil fuels. US researchers say corals can help to close this knowledge gap. Julia Cole, a climate scientist and paleoclimatologist at the University of Michigan, and her team recently published a study on this subject in the journal Science. "We've known for a long time that the last 40 or 50 years has really strong El Nino events," says Cole. "It's been hard to say whether the recent strong El Nino that we've had is part of a natural cycle, or if it's something a little bit unusual related to being in a warmer than normal world." The coral analysis points firmly in one direction: Unusual. Not normal. Corals: A repository of 1,000 years of climate history Cole and her team examined fossilized and living corals around the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador in the eastern Pacific. Corals grow between one and two centimeters per year, and in doing so form a structure similar to growth rings on trees. "We took advantage of the fact that corals, as they grow, preserve a record of ocean temperatures in the chemistry of their skeletons," Cole explains. Corals are living creatures that construct external skeletons through calcification, adding a band of new growth each year with calcium carbonate precipitated from the surrounding water. In this way, over decades and centuries, corals have formed entire reef systems. Other chemical elements are also incorporated into the skeleton during the calcification process — strontium, for example. Sometimes more is deposited, sometimes less, depending on the temperature of the water. The skeleton "takes in more strontium when it's colder, and it takes in less strontium when it's warmer," says Cole. The ratio of strontium to calcium in the skeleton provides information about changes in temperature. Specific isotopes of oxygen in coral skeletons provide clues, as well. "The rare oxygen-18 and the common oxygen-16 are also taken up in a ratio that reflects temperature," says Cole. In colder conditions, more oxygen-18 is absorbed than in warmer temperatures. In this way, researchers were able to reconstruct the changes in ocean temperatures over the past 1,000 years, according to the age of the corals. Their conclusion was that El Nino events have become markedly stronger compared to the pre-industrial period. Corals give indications, not conclusive answers Cole's study has confirmed a long-held suspicion. "These developments correspond to the predictions of the best climate models. They predict a quantifiably higher likelihood of extreme eastern Pacific El Nino events in the 2030s," says Jens Zinke, professor of paleobiology at the University of Leicester in England. However, other scientists are more circumspect in assessing the study's significance. "Coral data does achieve a high temporal resolution — monthly to seasonal — but its accuracy is dependent on local conditions, meaning that direct comparisons with modern measurement data are fraught with uncertainty," says Andreas Fink, professor of meteorology at the Institute for Meteorology and Climate Research in Karlsruhe. According to Fink, the significance of the study is undermined by its regional limitation to the eastern Pacific. Cole is also aware of her study's limitations. "Our data does fill a gap, but I want to be clear that our record isn't continuous," she says. "We don't have every single year over the last millennium. We have a little bit under half of the years covered." Floods, droughts, record heat — the consequences of stronger El Ninos Although the epicenter of the El Nino phenomenon is the Pacific, it changes the weather across the globe. In countries like Ecuador and Peru it can cause heavy rains and flooding, while Australia and Indonesia may experience a lack of rain, leading to drought and wildfires. El Niño also causes global temperatures to rise for a while. If the predictions prove right and this El Nino does in fact become a Super El Nino, the coming year, 2027, will probably be another of record heatwaves, according to Thomas Felis. Felis leads the research group on coral paleoclimatology at the MARUM Center for Marine Environmental Sciences at the University of Bremen, and has conducted a similar study to Cole's. Heat-stressed oceans: El Nino is a threat for corals A year of record heat "will very probably lead to another global coral bleaching," says Felis. This has happened before, in the years 2023–24 and 2015–16, which were also El Nino years. Corals get their characteristic colors from certain algae with which they live in symbiosis. Through photosynthesis, the algae provide the energy the corals need to live. If the temperature of the ocean is too high, the algae start to produce toxins, and the corals end the partnership. The coral remains, in its skeleton. It can survive like that for a few weeks, and if the temperature drops again, the algae return. "But if this state, with abnormally high summer temperatures, goes on for too long, the coral becomes so sick that it eventually dies," Felis explains. Worldwide coral death would mean not just the end of a unique ecosystem, but the destruction of an archive that preserves the history of the oceans. This article has been translated from German.

item.title: Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.32
Ukraine and Russia have signaled their readiness to resume trilateral talks under US mediation. "We're preparing. For October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president's office. Similar signals came from Moscow: "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner aimed to revive trilateral talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, visiting Moscow and Kyiv in the first week of September. The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved. Territory remains a difficult subject Vladimir Putin still demands more territory than Russia currently controls, Kushner confirmed on September 12, speaking online at the YES security conference in Kyiv. "President Putin [has] laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that," the US envoy said. The Ukrainian government has indicated it is willing to freeze the fighting along the current frontline in exchange for security guarantees. Such a step could be supported by 60% of Ukrainians, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted in summer 2026. A similar majority of respondents rejected giving up territory that Russia hasn't been able to conquer. 33% said Ukraine should give up territory that Putin demands. Russia's air superiority is a problem for Ukraine Few expect a breakthrough anytime soon. "For there to be a negotiated end to the war, there has to be parity. Right now, there's a stalemate on the front lines and not much is changing there, but in the air war, unfortunately, Russia currently has a significant advantage," Volodymyr Fesenko, a Kyiv-based political scientist, told DW. Ukraine is running low on interceptors for Russian ballistic missiles. Russia has also stepped up attacks with new jet-powered drones, which fly faster than older gasoline-powered models and are harder to intercept. Russian airstrikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine's economy, including warehouses, energy facilities, gas stations and railway infrastructure. The Kremlin has accused Ukraine of opening a "Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and fuel and energy facilities with deep strikes since the summer. Ukraine says the attacks are intended to force Russia to the negotiating table. Ukraine is worrying about the winter Ukraine's supporters say Kyiv's strategy is working. "The escalation ... is not a problem. It's a sign of success," said Jonathan Powell, the United Kingdom's National Security Adviser, speaking at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on September 11. "Of course [Putin] doesn't go straight to negotiations, he tries to escalate in the ways that he can." The West must "keep its foot on the gas" to make Putin negotiate in earnest, Powell said. Such optimism contrasts with concerns in Ukraine about the upcoming winter. In 2025, Russian attacks on energy infrastructure caused extended blackouts and left people without heating in freezing temperatures. "We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country," said Ukraine's Economy Minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko. Zelenskyy calls for partial de-escalation Russia rejected the idea of a ceasefire during the upcoming talks. Ukraine is now calling for a de-escalation of attacks on energy infrastructure and the unblocking of grain exports via the Black Sea instead. "What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So, energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told DW in an interview aired on September 12. Political scientist Fesenko says an agreement on grain exports could prove the easier task: "In the Black Sea, both Ukraine and Russia are facing major problems. Grain exports have been blocked; ports have been shut down and therefore both sides have a stake in the matter." An energy truce, however, remains elusive, as Ukraine's vulnerability in the winter gives Putin leverage he would not give up easily, Fesenko said. At the same time, the US is increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy facilities. "Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Donald Trump said on Sunday. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world." A day later, Trump claimed on social media that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy truce. “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. However, neither Ukraine nor Russia immediately confirmed the reported agreement. Kremlin rejected Zelenskyy-Putin meeting The Kremlin has already rejected another of Zelenskyy's proposals: a meeting between the Ukrainian and Russian leaders in December on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Miami. "Putin doesn't want to negotiate with Zelenskyy. It's been obvious since last year that he wants to reach an agreement with Trump," said Fesenko. "If Trump insists, Putin may agree to a meeting between the three leaders. But he has no intention of negotiating with Zelenskyy." If negotiations start in October as expected, negotiating teams rather than the leaders themselves will conduct them. But Ukraine insists that only the presidents can decide the territorial issue. "The territorial question remains a pressing one... Complex issues such as this are only resolved at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said during the US envoys' visit to Kyiv. Edited by: Carla Bleiker This article was updated to include a claim by Donald Trump that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking energy targets. Neither government immediately publicly confirmed that.

item.title: Nepal: thousands still missing as flood recovery begins
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.17
Nearly three weeks after deadly flash floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border, the Himalayan nation is shifting from search-and-rescue operations to relief and reconstruction efforts. Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,386 bodies have been recovered across five affected districts, while more than 5,130 people are still missing. The latter figure includes 587 foreign nationals and around 900 workers employed in hydropower tunnels and other energy facilities. The deluge, which authorities say was triggered by a glacier collapse, devastated communities and swept away more than a dozen hydropower facilities. As search operations continue in submerged tunnels and along muddy riverbanks, families are growing increasingly desperate for news of missing loved ones. Villages wiped out in minutes The scale of human loss is particularly stark in the upper river basins, where entire settlements vanished within minutes. In many places, destroyed roads and bridges have cut off access, forcing rescue and relief teams to rely on helicopters to deliver essential supplies. Niranjan Paudyal, a resident of Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District who lost his parents, uncle, aunt and sister in the flash floods, said the flood took away even the chance of burying his family members. "We spent days searching through debris, hoping for signs of my missing parents and family," he told DW. "Sadly, the disaster left us with no choice but to perform their final rites without their bodies." Public land in Uttargaya Rural Municipality in Rasuwa District has either been washed away or rendered unsafe. "There is not even land left after the flood to perform the final rites of those who lost their lives," Chameli Gurung, the municipality's deputy chair, told DW. "Relatives have to travel to Kathmandu's Pashupati Aryaghat to perform the final rites." In Uttargaya alone, at least 618 houses were swept away or buried and 877 people remain missing. Only 12 bodies have been recovered. Gurung said local authorities are exploring the possibility of leasing private land to accommodate displaced families before winter. Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, told DW that affected people are being resettled close to their original homes by securing nearby public or private land and providing financial assistance based on household size until they can become self-reliant. Nepal faced with a colossal recovery bill As emergency relief efforts begin to stabilize, Nepal faces a massive financial burden. A preliminary rapid damage and needs assessment (RDNA) puts the total reconstruction requirement at about 723.3 billion Nepalese rupees ($4.8 billion, €4.2 billion), according to local media reports. The RDNA estimates that nearly two thirds of the funds will go into restoring energy and transport networks and academic facilities. Hydropower, which supplies almost all of Nepal's electricity, had become a fast-growing source of the country's export revenue. The flood damage has deepened concerns about how Nepal will finance its recovery. On Monday, neighboring India approved the export of power to Nepal for 18 hours a day until at least December 31, Reuters news agency reported. "We will try to utilize all of our domestic resources and seek international support to manage the funding gaps," Timilsina, the communication minister, told DW. Nepal wants to grow resilient Nepal has formally approached the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed Loss and Damage Fund for assistance. However, the fund, established to help countries deal with the impacts of climate change, has yet to begin distributing its limited resources. Nepal is seeking to turn reconstruction into part of a broader economic recovery strategy, with an emphasis on climate-resilient infrastructure rather than simply replacing what was destroyed. "Given our previous experience with post-disaster management, what matters most is how effectively we can use the funds to restore lives and livelihoods and build disaster-resilient infrastructure," Roshee Lamichhane, an associate professor at Kathmandu University, told DW. Demand for climate justice Beyond recovery finance, Nepal is making a broader climate justice argument on the international stage. Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 24, where he is expected to call for global responsibility for mitigating climate impacts. Despite contributing less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal remains highly vulnerable to climate-induced hazards. "Reconstruction would be used as an opportunity to build climate-resilient infrastructure," Maheshwar Dhakal, who leads the Climate Change Management Division at Nepal's Ministry of Forests and Environment, told DW. "We will develop a guideline with the motto of 'tomorrow for a better future.'" Climate scientists caution against attributing any single extreme event solely to global warming without detailed studies, but they agree that rising temperatures are accelerating glacial melt across the Himalayas. Manjeet Dhakal, director of Climate Analytics South Asia, says the scale of the disaster highlights the growing consequences of rising global temperatures and gives Nepal an opportunity to advocate for cuts in global carbon emissions on the international stage. "How many more disasters should we wait for before there is a global response to address the impacts of climate change?" he asked, adding that developed and advanced countries, alongside other nations, should take greater responsibility. Edited by: Keith Walker

item.title: China tightens travel rules over tech security
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.72
