Sweeping travel restrictions on Chinese citizens came into effect on Tuesday, including exit bans for people considered to have endangered China's "industrial or technological security." The new exit-and-entry rules, which were passed in July, apply to citizens deemed to have violated technology import and export regulations, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence. The State Council in Beijing said the new rules were formulated to "safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests." The regulations apply not only to people within China but also to Chinese citizens deemed to have committed criminal acts abroad. In such cases, citizens could be "prohibited from leaving the country for a period of six months to three years from the date of their return to China," said the State Council. Travel bans give Beijing 'wide remit' The restrictions come as China remains locked in a technological arms race with the United States, with both countries accusing each other of stealing locally developed AI models in recent months. And analysts warn that the full scope of the new rules will only become clear once they start being implemented. Security and criminal activities "can be vaguely defined and easily adjusted," said Chong Ja Ian, an analyst from the National University of Singapore, telling the AFP news agency that Beijing has given itself a "wide remit." Will China's new travel bans affect foreigners? Under the new regulations, foreign nationals could also be denied entry to China for up to five years if found to have made false statements in visa applications. Foreign governments have often reported instances of citizens being denied permission to leave China due to security-related investigations. Analyst Chong highlighted the recent case of US citizen Min Zin who the US government said was detained improperly in Yunnan province in June. "The case of Min Zin is a reminder that the range of people [that Beijing] could restrict from exiting could be quite wide – and potentially arbitrary," he said. Chinese travel bans: Taiwan warns citizens The new rules could have particular implications for Taiwanese nationals who work in the tech sector and who travel between Taiwan and China. Authorities in Taipei have warned citizens to take extra care on visits to China, which considers people from Taiwan to be Chinese citizens. Beijing has dismissed any such concerns, claiming the rules provide better legal protection for Taiwanese. Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told AFP the travel restrictions "send a message" that China will take action to prevent "leaks in security or national interest-sensitive areas." Edited by: Natalie Muller If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Finland: EU leaders meet to forge new Arctic policy
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.66
European leaders gathered in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Monday to plan a path forward for the bloc's presence in the Arctic. The talks focused on emerging shipping lanes, raw mineral deposits and security threats from the US, China and Russia. They come as Arctic ice melts and northern waters become easier to navigate, and in the wake of US President Donald Trump's calls for the US to take control of Greenland which put severe strain on the NATO alliance. Call for a 'more strategic and proactive' EU role in Arctic German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and 11 other EU leaders issued a joint statement amid Monday's meeting well to the north of Helsinki headed towards the Arctic coastline. "We agree that the EU needs to step up its action to promote stability, sustainable development and prosperity while safeguarding its interests," the statement said. "We call for the European Union to take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic," the declaration urged. Besides Merz and Germany, the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Estonia, France, Greece, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden backed the statement. They called for improved monitoring and information-sharing, increasing investment in transport links, digital networks military mobility and other infrastrure. The statement also emphasized addressing hybrid threats and protecting critical infrastructure on land and sea. Senior EU officials Kaja Kallas and Antonio Costa also attended the session. EU using meeting to shape its new Arctic strategy No formal decisions were expected on Monday, but the European Commission said the talks would help shape its new Arctic strategy, which will be unveiled over the next few weeks. National leaders can still have a say impacting the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," said Tuomas Tikkanen — Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's senior adviser on European affairs. The bloc's last strategy paper was released in 2021. "The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably," Orpo, who initiated the summit, has emphasized that the Arctic is an, "increasingly important part of Europe's security environment." The Arctic, which is warming nearly four times faster than other regions, has seen increased activity as receding ice opens potential transport routes as well as access to mineral resources. The EU's foreign policy chief Kallas echoed sentiments of host Finland's government, saying that Brussels needed icebreaker vessels to boost its Arctic presence. Kallas said that given "the situation we are in, and considering also climate change and the opening of maritime routes, we need icebreakers or ships that are able to navigate" in still-difficult conditions in the polar region. The changing environment has spurred the US, China and Russia to increase energy, resource and military activity. In August, China and South Korea both sent container ships through the region, testing the viability of the North Sea Route in Russian territorial waters. As Arctic ice melts, desire for control of the Arctic has heated up Although Canada, China, Russia and Scandinavian countries are all considered Arctic nations, the most concerning development of late for the EU and member state Denmark have come from an entirely unexpected corner — the United States. US President Donald Trump has put severe strain on the NATO military alliance through his insistence that "the US must have Greenland" — a semi-autonomous island nation that is officially Danish territory — citing national security concerns. Trump previously argued that Denmark cannot protect Greenland, which is not part of the EU, from China and Russia. The US, Denmark and Greenland have set up a working group to discuss how to proceed, with Danish Prime Minsiter Mette Frederiksen expressing hope for the process on Monday. "This working group is still working and therefore it's too early to draw any conclusions but I'm quite optimistic that we can find a way," she told reporters. The US wants to increase its military presence on Greenland, something past treaties enable it to do, after decades of reducing its military footprint there since the end of the Cold War. NATO has also launched a new security mission in the region in recent months. Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, on a visit to Greenland, announced closer cooperation and an investment package of €200 million ($231 million) to be used in part to set up infrastructure to extract valuable raw materials. During her visit, von der Leyen said that the EU would "be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic," saying the package would "create new opportunities and a strong and engaged EU in both Greenland and the Arctic." Edited by: Natalie Muller If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Pay to ghost your boss: Japan's resignation business
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.15
For Y.M., a Japanese man in his early 20s, his first job out of university at a real estate sales firm quickly turned into a daily trial of endurance. Among his colleagues, he was always the one being screamed at. According to his testimony featured on the website of Leadbrain, a Tokyo-based labor and human resources consulting firm, he sought a quiet way out because he was wary of how colleagues perceived him. He was reluctant to burden his parents and determined to avoid workplace conflict, which is a common attitude among working Japanese. Rather than submitting his resignation in person, he opened his phone and began searching for a resignation proxy service, a third-party agency that could help him quit without direct interaction with his employer. In Japan, vanishing from a workplace without notice is known as bakkure, a concept somewhat parallel to "ghosting" in modern dating. For many foreigners, leaving a job without notice would be considered an irresponsible and hurtful act. But within the logic of Japanese social interactions, vanishing is a way to avoid direct conflict and maintain harmony — at least on the outside. Pay to flee Demand for these resignation agencies is booming. Albatross, one of Japan's leading businesses of this kind, helps about 450 people quit without confrontation every month. They charge roughly €120 ($138.5) per client working a full-time job. The majority of these clients are young professionals in the service industry and manufacturing. The process can be completed within 15 minutes. "The reasons why people requested us to resign for them range from physical violence to sexual harassment," said Yuka Hamada, the CEO of Albatross. "They are vulnerable in this case, and they are not brave enough to quit their job." Around one in three people reported experiencing some form of harassment at work, according to a survey of Japanese workers aged 20 to 49 by consulting firm Shikigaku. Harmony above all else Traditional Japanese corporate culture originated during the post-World War II economic boom and relies heavily on the "lifetime employment" system. In this culture, loyalty is regarded as the highest virtue, and bosses often view resignations as insults, so many young employees fear resigning in person. "Announcing one's intention to resign can feel not merely like ending a contract, but like disappointing others or betraying expectations that one has previously continued to meet," said Hiroki Nakamori, an associate professor at Rikkyo University's Graduate School of Social Design Studies. Japan is a non-confrontational culture, and people are expected to fall in line when making certain commitments to the company and its culture. "Those who disturb the harmony are not appreciated, so someone leaving might feel they should just disappear without making too much of a fuss," said Hiroshi Ono, a professor of Human Resources Management at Hitotsubashi University Business School. "Acting in a collective and acting in harmony is a sign of strength." This cultural compulsion to avoid conflict runs deep. Even Japan's 17-Article Constitution, the 7th century foundation of modern Japanese governance, explicitly states: "Harmony should be valued and quarrels should be avoided." Ghosting with consideration But you can also politely ghost a job. "Clients may not say goodbye or express their gratitude directly to the company. In such cases, the agency can deliver these words on their behalf," says Albatross CEO Hamada. It is the ultimate paradox of Japanese workplace culture: Even when ghosting, the employee feels compelled to abide by meiwaku — the social obligation to minimize trouble for others and preserve collective order above all else. This also applies to removing their personal items from the workplace. "Even if a client intends to completely vanish from their job, we still advise them to clear off their desk" before leaving, added Hamada. Edited by: Darko Janjevic

item.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.09
The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero's farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia's accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive. "For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country," Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade's continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law. Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia's Institute for European Affairs adds: "The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years." A candidate moving away from Europe Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense. Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning. Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia. Has the EU been too lenient? But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values. Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye. Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia's largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow. A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China. Strong economic ties, close relations with Russia Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues. Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action. Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe. The limits of financial pressure The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence. Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic's calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country's democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions. Could the election bring change? The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic's model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia's dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister. Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that "it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections." Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia's institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU. Reconciliation remains a distant prospect Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media. "What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years," Morina underlines. Mladic's funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership. Edited by: Carla Bleiker

item.title: Magyar vs. Moscow: Hungary toughens stance toward Russia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.98
While Viktor Orban was in power, no other EU member state was as pro-Russia as Hungary. Indeed, the prime minister's apparent eagerness to be of service to the Russian president earned him the nickname "Putin's pinscher" or "Kremlin agent." For years, Hungary was seen as a security risk both in the EU and NATO. Russian spies were able to operate in the country largely unhindered for a long time. In February, it came to light that Peter Szijjarto, Orban's foreign minister from 2014 to 2026, had passed on confidential information from EU meetings to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov. All this came to an end in May, when the government headed by Peter Magyar took office. An unambiguous signal to Russia In a clear departure from the government line under Orban, Hungary's new prime minister has already heavily criticized Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine several times. The government also recently declared Russia a threat to Hungary's national security. This week, it took its biggest step yet against the Kremlin, expelling 10 Russian diplomats for engaging in activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," as announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban (no relation to the former prime minister). Although Orban did not provide any more details, the phrase is generally understood to mean that the diplomats in question were spies. Orban said the decision "protects Hungary's security and sovereignty." She added: "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules." Restoring old alliances The minister's brief announcement immediately generated a huge number of headlines and comments — hardly surprising given that this was not only evidence of a 180-degree turn on the government's policy toward Russia but also one of the toughest diplomatic sanctions targeting Moscow since the collapse of communism in 1989/1990. Speaking to Hungarian news website Index, secret service expert Peter Tarjani said this was "not a diplomatic conflict, but a serious secret service matter" and that with this decision, Hungary was simultaneously returning "to the mainstream of its allies' security policy." Political scientist and leading Hungarian Russia expert Andras Racz told the Hungarian national news agency MTI that Hungary was the only EU and NATO member not to have made such an expulsion in recent years. Racz said such a step "should really have been taken four and ahalf years ago." He added: "Hungary is now settling its old debt with its allies." Reliance on Russian gas? Under Viktor Orban, Hungary was the only EU country never to unreservedly condemn Russia's all-out war against Ukraine. Indeed, during the final two years of his rule, Orban even blamed Ukraine and the West for Russia's aggression. But long before that — even after he came to power back in 2010 — Viktor Orban took a markedly pro-Russia line, which he justified, among other things, with the claim that Hungary was more dependent on Russian energy supplies than almost any other country in the region. His government's repeated assertion that Russian gas was cheaper has long been disproved. What's more, the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant with Russian support will cost Hungary dearly for decades to come. In the light of all this, Orban's close ties to Russia remain a mystery. Absurd situations For Hungary, this closeness to Russia often led to absurd situations in which the country's national security was put at risk. At the same time, Orban repeatedly told his critics that it was they who were a threat to Hungary's sovereignty. For example, Russian secret service agents for years took part in military-style training exercises in the far-right scene right up until 2016. Starting in 2012, Russian secret service operatives for years stole huge amounts of data from the Hungarian Foreign Ministry and other agencies without the government ever publicly condemning it. In 2019, Russia got permission to move the headquarters of the International Investment Bank (IIB) to Budapest. The IIB was known as the "spy bank" because its leadership was made up of individuals linked to or associated with Russia's FSB intelligence service. It was only after the United States imposed sanctions on the bank in 2023 that it left Hungary again. Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has warned multiple times in recent years that Hungary had become a "logistical center and deployment zone for Russian secret services," thereby putting the whole region at risk. Rejection of Orban's pro-Russia course Orban's strictly pro-Russia course was laterally rejected by many Hungarians. The decidedly pro-EU orientation of Peter Magyar and his Tisza party had a considerable role to play in the party's election victory earlier this year. The EU flag was often seen and spontaneous cries of "Russians, go home" were often heard at election rallies last spring. Unlike Viktor Orban, Magyar and leading Tisza politicians are convinced that Hungary's place is exclusively in the European Union and that the country should only maintain pragmatic low-level relations with Russia. Nevertheless, many observers and experts are surprised at how radically the Magyar government has turned away from Russia. Andras Telkes, the former deputy head of Hungary's foreign intelligence service (IH), wrote in the newspaper Nepszava that the expulsion of diplomats shows that the presence of Russian secret services in Hungary obviously runs "very deep" and that the country has a serious problem. Telkes said the expulsion of 10 diplomats would help rebuild trust in Hungary in the eyes of the secret services of its NATO allies. He said the decision was significant. "Expelling two or three people would have been a sign," Telkes said. "Expelling 10 people already means war." Telkes said the expulsions create a serious security problem for Hungary. Will Moscow turn off the taps? A spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry condemned the expulsion of the diplomats in strong terms. She spoke of a "Russophobe lobby in Budapest" and announced a "hard and painful" response. Russian lawmaker Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma's Defense Committee, said the government would consider halting gas supplies to Hungary. Foreign Minister Orban knows more about such Russian threats than anyone else in the new Hungarian government: In 2007, she wrote her doctoral thesis on Russia's energy policy in Central Europe. A year later, she published a book: "Power, Energy, and the New Russian Imperialism." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.93
Several top EU politicians have called a Russian drone strike on a passenger train on Ukraine's border with Poland a bid by Moscow to intimidate Kyiv's allies that should be met with even more resolution. In the incident, a drone hit the train's locomotive at a railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border, shortly after a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European diplomats had been at the station. What did EU leaders say about the train attack? "It [the attack] is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said. "I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared," she told reporters in Finland, where she attended a summit on Arctic strategy. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who was also at the meeting, said the attack demonstrated Russia's growing aggression and called both for more support for Kyiv and for harsher penalties on Moscow. "For me, it means that we have to [...] do even more to help Ukraine, to support Ukraine. And we need more measures against Russia, more political measures, more sanctions, and make it clear that this is strong strategy," he said. "We are united here in Europe," he added. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said the attack showed that Russia was "challenging all of us." "We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it," he said. French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack had a "very clear goal, which is to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, drive a wedge between them." Barrot said Russian President Vladimir Putin had constantly stepped up pressure on the EU and NATO over the past five years. "Why? Because he knows that our strength lies in our unity, and that as long as we stand together, nothing can intimidate us," he said. Germany warns against escalation with Russia German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius, for his part, called for caution. "I take the drones that were approaching trains near the (Ukrainian-Polish) border very seriously, but we must not be forced into an escalation," he said. The Kremlin has commented on the attack only by saying that the Russian army operated across all Ukrainian territory and would continue to do so. Speaking about the incident on Sunday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has said Putin considered Russia to be "de facto" at war with Europe. "Putin's terror is literally knocking at the door of the European Union and NATO," Sybiga said. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Russia's attack would drive the transatlantic alliance to keep on pushing its support for Ukraine. “Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," Rutte said at NATO's offices in Brussels, adding a call to increase support for Kyiv. According to Rutte, Russian leader Putin "thinks he can stop" NATO from supporting Ukraine. "He is wrong." Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.80
A drone which entered Lithuanian airspace in the early hours of Tuesday morning was shot down by NATO fighter jets in between the cities of Vilnius and Kaunas, Lithuanian authorities have confirmed. Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center (NKVC) said the drone most likely came from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Russia in its ongoing war against Ukraine, and was flying west when it was shot down by an Italian jet. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda thanked the military alliance for its "swift response." "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region," he wrote on social media. "Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace." Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said the NATO response sent "a clear message that NATO stands vigilant, committed, and ready." What do we know about the latest drone incident? Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the NKVC, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus and flew along the outskirts of populated areas for about 30 minutes before being intercepted. The Lithuanian armed forces published video from the site of the crash near the village of Pratkunai, close to Lithuania's second-largest city, Kaunas, and about 80 kilometers (50 miles) west of the capital, Vilnius. The footage showed debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood and some appeared charred. The commander of the Lithuanian air force, Antanas Matutis, said that the drone had "likely" been carrying explosives. Lithuania: Was the drone from Russia or Ukraine? Officials have not indicated whether the drone was Russian or Ukrainian. While Russia has been launching almost daily drone and missile strikes against Ukraine since the start of its full-scale invasion over four years ago, Ukraine has also been responding with drone strikes of its own. Ukrainian drones, which often pass close to Lithuanian, Latvian and Estonian airspace en route to targets in northwestern Russia, have occasionally been jammed by Russian defenses and steered off course into NATO airspace. Fighter jets with the NATO Baltic Air Defense mission have patrolled the skies over Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over Estonia in May, and over Latvia in June and August. The Lithuanian military said Tuesday's incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in its airspace. How has NATO responded? Tuesday's incident came less than 24 hours after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said that strikes "close to the alliance's territory" would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Ukraine. "Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," he said, adding that drone strikes and incursions near NATO territory showed Russian President Vladimir Putin's "desperation" and "desire to sow fear and terror." On Tuesday, Poland, a NATO ally and neighbor of Lithuania, also announced "aviation operations" had commenced in its airspace "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory." These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions," said authorities in Warsaw. Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr, are also currently building up a German armored brigade in Lithuania. The combat-ready and independently deployable force, comprising 4,800 troops, is expected to be operational by 2027. Edited by: Natalie Muller If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis attack Saudis, seize crucial Red Sea islands
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.25
Iranian-backed Houthi rebels on Monday announced they had captured Greater and Lesser Hanish Island in the southern Red Sea. The move bolsters the group's ability to choke traffic in another key global maritime shipping route as the ripple-effect of the war in Iran grows. The strategic advance comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces try to regain territory recently lost near the Bab el-Mandab Strait, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran has held closed since US President Donald Trump began bombing the Islamic Republic on February 28. The closure of the Hormuz Strait, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the US began hostilities, has led to a global economic and energy emergency, driving up prices around the world and forcing petro-monarchy Saudi Arabia to move its oil exports through Bab el-Mandab. But the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and last week seized strategic Mayun Island and the Red Sea port of Mokha, cutting off the alternative route. The capture of Greater and Lesser Hanish now puts even more pressure on Saudi shipments and thus global oil supplies and prices. Beyond putting the squeeze on Saudi Arabia — the Houthis' proxy enemy for backing the internationally recognized government in the Yemen's reignited civil war — it could also provide Iran added leverage in defending itself against the US. Houthi offensive continues to escalate as Iran war expands The Houthis pressed on with their offensive Monday, launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A spokesman for the group said the strikes had caused "significant damage" and had come in response to "more than 300 [Saudi] airstrikes in [Yemen over] the past five days." Despite being a longtime backer of the Houthis as part of its anti-Israel "axis of resistance," Tehran has denied any involvement in Yemen's revived civil war. "Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs," said Tehran's Foreign Ministry on Monday, with spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters the Houthis are "entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests." Yemen's civil war — dormant for four years until the conflict in Iran broke out — began in 2014, when Houthi rebels seized large parts of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, and forced the government to flee to Aden in the south. In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition aiding the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world. Concerning situation for US and its Saudi, Gulf State allies On Monday, Admiral Brad Cooper of US Central Command (CENTCOM) was in Jeddah to discuss "the latest developments in the region" with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. US news site Axios reports that Cooper has been in the kingdom since Thursday, dealing with urgent coordination meetings as the situation in the Red Sea escalates. US media outlets reported last week that President Trump had rejected a request by the crown prince for the US to directly intervene. Despite turning down the request to unleash US firepower, Trump reportedly agreed to provide intelligence sharing and targeting assistance. Iran blames Saudi Arabia for stalling Hormuz talks Iran on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of delaying talks aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign Ministry spokesman Baghaei called a meeting set to take place in Oman, a "real opportunity" to restore security in the region and added that an agreement between Iran and Oman on opening the passage had been finalized and would be announced later. Saudi Arabia reportedly has concerns over the lasting implications of a deal for the Strait of Hormuz and how it might negatively impact Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. Tehran says Riyadh is using Yemen as a "pretext" to delay talks on how the Strait will be governed now that the status quo has been upended by the US. Currently, the only secure routes allowing Saudi Arabia to deliver its oil to Asian markets are via the Suez Canal or around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope. On Monday, China's Foreign Ministry called attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure "unacceptable," saying Beijing is "deeply concerned" about further escalation. Edited by: Kieran Burke If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: How Does the World Really View China?
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.60
In July, the Pew Research Center found that for the first time in roughly two decades of global polling, the world now views China more favorably than the United States. The sentiment was not universal, but in 25 of the 36 countries surveyed this year, the percentage of respondents who gave favorable marks to China exceeded that for the United States, including several close U.S. allies. Some analysts have taken these findings as confirmation that the golden era of American soft power is over and China is ascendant. According to them, Trump’s policies on tariffs, aid, and allies have eroded the United States’ standing, opening the door for people across the world to switch their allegiance to China. But this interpretation, convenient as it may be, deserves more scrutiny. A closer examination of the data reveals that although global opinion of the United States has indeed plummeted and opinion of China has risen since 2022, most of the world still prefers the United States as an economic partner—including most of the countries that now view China in a more positive light. This is a critical distinction, since economic partnerships and interests tend to drive national policies. Indeed, it signals something more nuanced is happening than simply the end of American hegemony and an imminent age of Chinese global supremacy. The world’s increasingly pro-Chinese attitude is not meaningless. That more and more people think better of Beijing than of Washington could eventually prove important as Beijing seeks to build up its soft power. For now, however, what the numbers actually show is a world adjusting to the new reality of great-power competition, feeling forced to choose one side without the luxury of liking it. STILL ON TOP Favorability is, in essence, a feeling. When people are asked to say how favorably they view something, they are really being asked whether and how much they like it—and little else. Pew’s favorability question also asked only whether respondents hold a positive or a negative impression of China and the United States, not whether they liked one more than the other. Still, Beijing clearly came out on top in these questions. Favorable views of the United States fell significantly in 15 of the 24 countries surveyed in both 2025 and 2026. Moreover, in several U.S. ally countries, including Canada, France, Germany, Italy, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, favorability ratings are now at or near their lowest since Pew began polling in 2002. In contrast, China’s image has consistently improved in several Western countries. The percentage of Italian respondents with a favorable opinion of China, for instance, increased from 31 percent in 2022 to 51 percent in 2026. In Spain, China’s favorability rose from 37 percent in 2025 to 54 percent in 2026. Media outlets and observers have fixated on these numbers, but the same Pew survey asks another, more consequential question: “Is it more important for your country to have strong economic ties with China or with the United States?” This prompt forces respondents to weigh the two powers against each other and pick one. Critically, it asks them to consider not just how they feel about each country but also which they would rather work with. In 2025, the last year for which country-by-country, individual-level data is available, more respondents in 20 out of 24 countries chose economic ties with the United States over ties with China. In seven of those 20 countries, answers to the two questions diverged. More respondents in Canada, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey rated China more favorably than the United States, yet more people chose economic ties with the United States over China, sometimes by wide margins. In Sweden, for example, respondents preferred U.S. economic ties to Chinese economic ties by 48 percentage points. Turkish respondents rated China 13 percentage points more favorably than they did the United States but preferred economic ties with the United States by ten percentage points anyway. As the only country that favors Chinese economic ties but views the United States more favorably, Australia is an outlier. This is not much of a surprise given that China is already the country’s largest export destination, accounting for 30 percent of everything Australia sells to the world. But it is noteworthy that half of Australians believe China is the country that threatens Australia most, and a full third believe the United States is Australia’s most important ally, compared with seven percent who believe China is. When asked, however, whether Australia’s economy should have closer ties to China or to the United States, 54 percent picked China, compared with 43 percent that picked the United States. Favorability, it appears, cannot adequately capture the nuance of public opinion on the two countries, much less divine a shift in the balance of soft power. Globally, the individual respondents who preferred China as an economic partner seem to have done so because they believe that China is already the world’s leading economic power. Sixty percent of global respondents who preferred economic ties with China believed as much, compared with 20 percent who think the United States is the world’s leading economic power. The same pattern holds true for the United States: roughly 58 percent of the people who prefer economic ties with the United States think that it is the global economic hegemon, whereas 26 percent believe that China is. This makes intuitive sense: people want to partner with whoever they think is the winner. But Pew’s data also suggests that people still have a desire to partner with Washington on economic matters, because many still say they want to even when they don’t think it is the winner. Of those who believe the United States still leads the world economy, 75 percent chose economic ties with the United States, compared with just 15 percent who chose a closer economic relationship with China. Yet among those who believe China has taken the lead, 49 percent chose China and a remarkable 38 percent still chose the United States. THE FENCE SITTERS Not everyone feels compelled to choose between the United States and China. Across the 24 countries surveyed in 2025, roughly one in nine respondents preferred that their country maintain strong economic ties with both powers rather than supporting one over the other. In some countries, this group of fence sitters is too large to ignore. Thirty-nine percent of Nigerians—a plurality of respondents—declined to choose between Washington and Beijing. So did 32 percent of Israelis, 27 percent of Hungarians, 23 percent of Germans, and 20 percent of Turks. Across all countries, 16 percent of those who named the United States as their country’s most important ally but believed China now leads the world economy opted not to choose a single most important economic partner, compared with 11 percent of all other respondents. That is not to say that fence-sitting publics will remain undecided as the U.S.-Chinese competition intensifies. They may yet be moved to commit to a side if it looks like a reliable protector against a clear danger. For Washington, this is still good news. In 20 of the 24 countries surveyed, more people named the United States than China as their country’s most important ally. China leads in only Indonesia, Nigeria, South Africa, and Turkey. In no country did a majority name China, whereas the United States won majorities in five countries. That gap is Beijing’s weakness and Washington’s remaining advantage. The Trump administration’s wavering commitment to allies threatens to undermine it. So might the common—and incorrect—belief that China has already won the economic race. By most measures, the U.S. economy is still the world’s largest and most productive. Yet in the eyes of the rest of the world, every new trade war and every rupture with an ally risks reinforcing the belief that the U.S. economy is headed in the wrong direction. For now, however, fears that public opinion has tilted toward China are overblown. When forced to choose, most of the world still prefers working with Washington, and most of those who choose Beijing are likely betting on predictions about its economic rise. Beijing, then, should not mistake favorability for partnership. And Washington must keep the United States’ markets open and its commitments credible before the belief that the country’s economic future is behind it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. item.title: The Case for a Stalemate With Iran
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.30
Six months in, the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran has settled into a stalemate. Neither Washington nor Tehran can achieve a clear military or diplomatic victory. Instead, the two sides have found themselves locked in a mutual blockade of oil and other shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and into Iranian ports, with no obvious way to change the status quo. The costs of accommodating the other side’s demands to end the stalemate are so high, and the costs of the stalemate sufficiently low, that a mutual blockade has emerged as the least bad option for both the United States and Iran for the foreseeable future. This situation may not be ideal for Washington, but it avoids both defeat and escalation. It also works to the United States’ advantage over time: as the blockade drags on, Tehran’s position is likely to weaken faster than Washington’s. The United States has its own ample oil supplies to draw from, whereas nearly the entirety of Iran’s oil exports—and therefore much of its hard currency—has been cut off. An ongoing blockade that gradually ratchets up pressure on Iran could make Tehran more flexible in negotiations with the United States, leading to a compromise that Washington could accept. The challenge is to ensure that Tehran does not choose to respond to its worsening position by escalating its attacks and starting another regionwide conflict that ensnares the United States. U.S. policy should focus on avoiding the most disruptive contingencies, especially Iranian escalation, and settle for maintaining dual blockades indefinitely. If Iran is unwilling to concede, Washington can slowly erode the Iranian economy and military while ensuring that Tehran cannot rebuild the strong regional position it enjoyed before the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. At this stage, maintaining the current U.S. position is the most effective way of fighting—and winning—this war. BEST OF THE WORST In June, Washington and Tehran agreed to a memorandum of understanding to first establish a cease-fire and open the Strait of Hormuz and then to sign a permanent deal within 60 days to resolve long-term issues in the bilateral relationship, including restricting Iran’s nuclear program and removing U.S. and international sanctions and other financial penalties on Iran. But it fell apart before a final deal could be reached largely because Iran failed to fully open the strait. With diplomatic solutions going nowhere, both Washington and Tehran are now hoping that the economic pressure each can put on the other—and in the case of Iran, on the global economy—will force its counterpart back to the negotiating table on terms that will resolve the blockade in its favor. A blockade comes with costs for Washington. Keeping the strait closed is raising gas prices and increasing inflation in the United States, an especially sensitive issue as the November midterm elections approach. Prices could rise further if Iran finds a way to limit the millions of barrels of oil that bypass its blockade and are transported through the Strait of Hormuz daily. And the United States has already used up many critical munitions and strained its troops in the region by keeping the war going. But the operation has been relatively affordable compared with past conflicts. The United States lost thousands of lives and spent trillions of dollars in Afghanistan and Iraq, whereas the ongoing conflict with Iran has resulted in 18 American service members killed and has likely cost tens of billions of dollars. (As of mid-July, estimates ranged from $37.5 billion to over $100 billion.) Most important, the mutual blockade has the advantage of being more palatable to political leaders in Washington than any of the alternative options. A full U.S. withdrawal from the Strait of Hormuz without gaining concessions from Iran, including ending its blockade, would be unthinkable even for the unorthodox Trump administration. It would allow Iran to tout a complete victory and give the regime in Tehran a powerful psychological boost that would undo much of the progress that the United States and Israel made in the past three years decimating Iran’s network of regional proxies. And it would probably not lead Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz for free passage—Tehran is likely to insist on installing some kind of tolling system in perpetuity. With Washington in retreat, Iran could also revive and rebuild its nuclear program, which would be a stunning failure for the United States. The United States can continue the mutual blockade at relatively low cost. Military escalation is an even less appealing option for Washington. The Iranian regime has already survived a massive bombing campaign; a new, even more aggressive offensive could take out much of Iran’s remaining military capabilities and its energy, transportation, and communications infrastructure, but such an offensive could not guarantee that Tehran would accept American terms on opening the strait or curtailing its nuclear program. Having already weathered so many attacks aimed at diminishing its power, the remaining Iranian leadership, which learned to tolerate hardship in the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, is unlikely to be cowed by further aggression. Moreover, it could retaliate by targeting Gulf Arab states’ infrastructure and depleting remaining U.S. air defense missiles, which would raise the costs of the war to the United States and its partners. The other option for the United States is a land invasion aimed at forcibly ousting the Iranian regime. This would require a military effort likely as large as the 1991 Desert Storm operation, which involved more than 500,000 American troops. Such an operation risks the significant loss of American life, huge costs to Iranian civilians, and disorder across the entire region. The Trump administration, which has consistently derided prior U.S. “forever wars” in the Middle East, appears to have ruled this option out months ago. Washington’s calculation, then, is that a blockade is preferable to any other alternative. The blockade serves as a slow-moving pressure campaign either to bring Iran back to the negotiating table to agree to something along the lines of the compromise outlined in the June memorandum of understanding or to gradually weaken the Islamic Republic’s economic and military strength and eventually its internal stability. This type of campaign has a mixed historical record, but it worked in 1988 when, after eight years of war with Iraq and a failed naval confrontation with the United States in the Persian Gulf, Iran ended hostilities by withdrawing its troops from Iraq. So far, the costs of the mutual blockade have been tolerable for the United States. Despite six months of an almost continuous Gulf oil and natural gas embargo by Iran, the global economy is suffering minimal damage. In July, five months into the war, the International Monetary Fund revised its 2026 global GDP growth estimates downward only 0.1 percentage point—from 3.1 percent to 3.0 percent—“with limited evidence of second round effects” of the oil shock. American gasoline prices have risen about 38 percent over the course of the war, but the country’s economic growth rate remains steady. Deeper shortages could push gas prices higher, but because the United States now produces more oil than it consumes, Washington could intervene in the market to keep prices down. In this context, the United States can continue the mutual blockade at relatively low cost. STUCK IN THE MIDDLE WITH YOU The leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have held on to power so far—and seem poised to stay in power indefinitely. They have shifted Iran to a crisis economy, tightening their grip on the population and protecting their military programs at the expense of the Iranian people. They do not want to concede to terms like those in the memorandum of understanding because doing so would cost them their last major weapon—the ability to close the strait—and make them face possible new restrictions on their nuclear program. (In the June memorandum, for example, Tehran only vaguely committed to dilute its highly enriched uranium, which is Washington’s priority in reducing the Iranian nuclear threat.) The United States, however, has time on its side. If Washington maintains its blockade through November’s election, the strategic value of the closure to Iran will decline as flights and tourist travel drop from summer highs and as countries improve their coping strategies by finding alternative energy suppliers. And in Iran, the effects of the blockade on its oil exports are already being felt. Inflation rose to over 80 percent year-over-year in August, and the value of the currency has been dropping rapidly. Iran’s leadership may be hardened by war, but the country’s economy will eventually need oil exports and reduced sanctions to survive. The economic pressure has pushed some political leaders, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, to suggest a return to the terms of the memorandum of understanding with the United States. Iran’s economy will eventually need oil exports and reduced sanctions to survive. But if the pressure on the economy makes Tehran desperate, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps leaders who ultimately call the shots could choose to escalate the situation rather than seek compromise. Iran could crack down further on any U.S. efforts to squeeze ships through the strait, including by laying new mines (as it was preparing to do on August 30, prompting a U.S. strike), and it could attempt to shut down Saudi and Emirati pipelines that bypass the strait and channel millions of barrels of oil daily from the Gulf. Alternatively, in addition to its current sporadic attacks, Tehran could launch a major military offensive, using its remaining stocks of missiles and drones to destroy much of the Gulf Arab states’ infrastructure, damage U.S. bases and ships, and even strike Israel. If such an attack succeeds, Gulf Arab states’ need to save their huge oil infrastructure investments could knock them out of their informal American coalition or force Washington to accept Iranian terms on reopening the strait. If Iran escalated in this way, the Trump administration would have to retaliate militarily despite its reluctance to do so. According to foreign military sources, the United States and Israel had planned just such a massive air offensive in early August that would have been far larger and more damaging than earlier bombings. But Washington canceled the attack in part because of Gulf Arab states’ concerns about potential retaliation. Any of the scenarios is possible. Iran has traditionally chosen to escalate, but given how hard its economy and its proxies have been hit since 2023, it is possible that it is willing to negotiate rather than surrender. As the stalemate drags on, and if Washington does not budge, Iran’s leadership thus will eventually have to decide which of the three available options it wants to pursue: negotiating a compromise similar to the memorandum of understanding, raising the stakes with aggressive action, or prolonging the blockade while finding itself in an increasingly disadvantageous position. WINNING BY STALEMATE When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran in February, they could not foresee that six months later the result would be a double blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli and American leaders likely thought they would have destroyed the regime or forced Tehran to compromise. But now, given the alternatives, embracing the stalemate is the best possible option for the United States. The United States was unable to quickly defeat Iran, but it remains better able to absorb the costs of the current blockade as Iran’s economy slowly buckles under the strain. The biggest risk to an ongoing stalemate is if Iran decides to escalate. Washington needs to warn Iran of the severe consequences it would face if it were to launch a large offensive or restart its nuclear program. Only American power can deter Iran. Washington thus should play to a stalemate but be ready to respond with a truly devastating counteroffensive if Iran raises the stakes. With the U.S. position getting stronger over time, Iran’s only real advantages lie in pushing back just enough to avoid triggering such a U.S. response. A stalemate accompanied by the right threats can be a strategy for not only winning the war but also for solidifying and building on the essential gains Washington has made in its larger three-year conflict with Iran and its proxies. It will not transform the Middle East on its own, but by putting Iran in a weaker position, it could encourage much-needed restraint from Tehran. item.title: The Coming Risks to Russian Power
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.77
The United States has long viewed Russia as a power in terminal decline. This assessment formed in the 1980s as the Soviet Union began showing clear signs of imperial overstretch, and it congealed after the collapse of first the Warsaw Pact and then the Soviet Union itself. Washington went on to pursue a policy agenda, including NATO enlargement, that treated Russian power and interests as an afterthought, and the long-standing conflict over Ukraine turned dismissiveness into condescension. In March 2014, U.S. President Barack Obama called Russia “a regional power” that was “threatening some of its immediate neighbors, not out of strength but out of weakness.” President Donald Trump shows more fondness for Russian President Vladimir Putin than his predecessors did, but most Russia watchers in the West still dwell on Russia’s lagging technology; its failure to rescue allies in Syria, Venezuela, and Cuba; and what they see as its reduction to a vassal of mighty China. This picture of Russia as feeble and fading may suit the biases of Putin’s many critics, but it is fundamentally at odds with reality: Moscow consistently punches above its weight in global affairs. Thirty-five years after the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Russia remains a nuclear superpower. As during the Cold War, NATO treats it as the benchmark threat around which the alliance plans its forces. An unprecedented wall of Western sanctions has failed to trigger the economic collapse its architects predicted or to erode political and social stability. The effort to isolate Moscow has faltered as well. The Kremlin has skillfully promoted non-Western bodies such as BRICS, a grouping of major emerging economies, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a Eurasian political and security group. In so doing, it has extended its influence over the post-Western order now taking shape. And even though Russia’s economy is far smaller than China’s, the “no limits” partnership between Moscow and Beijing has produced a formidable coalition. This bullish assessment comes with a caveat: it relies on the international conditions that prevail today. Moscow continues to punch above its weight because it is navigating a fragmented, unpredictable world that plays to its strengths. Volatility and instability, active conflicts and arms races across several regions, economic decoupling and the retreat of globalization, the worldwide rise of nationalism and populism, the discounting of soft power and fissures in the Western alliance—all these features of the existing international order work to Moscow’s advantage. The downside risk for Russia is that today’s turmoil and uncertainty may not last. The pendulum is likely to swing back, with global disorder subsiding and the international system consolidating anew. That reversal could come when Trump leaves the White House, especially if his successor restores traditional U.S. support for the transatlantic alliance, multilateralism, and open trade. A planetary shock—accelerating climate change, an out-of-control AI system, or some other surprise—could likewise push states to set aside their current conflicts in favor of closer cooperation. When this change happens—and it will—Russia may find that its time-tested foreign policy and its once reliable but rigid institutions no longer serve it well. THRIVING IN CHAOS The centrifugal trends pulling the international system apart work to Moscow’s advantage. In a fragmented and dangerous world of strongmen, where raw power decides outcomes, Russia’s military heft remains a durable source of strength and influence. Russia is also the only power that can rival the United States in strategic nuclear weapons. China is modernizing and expanding its arsenal, but Beijing will need a long time to catch up with the two superpowers. Russia’s nuclear status has practical effects: it has deterred NATO members from deploying troops to Ukraine, and it gives Moscow powerful diplomatic leverage on arms control, strategic stability and risk reduction, nonproliferation, and the prevention of nuclear terrorism. As for its conventional capabilities, Russia retains a blue-water navy and long-range strike capabilities; only the United States can project power more widely. To be sure, the initial phase of fighting in Ukraine in February 2022 exposed serious weaknesses in the Russian army. But over the four and a half years since, the armed forces have transformed themselves, sharply improving their efficiency and combat power. Moscow now fields one of the world’s strongest militaries and, beyond that, has unique experience in next-generation ground warfare—an edge over almost any other fighting force, the United States included. Ukraine, too, has adapted its forces and tactics to new battle technologies, but it depends on Western support and may not be able to preserve those capabilities once the fighting stops. The accumulated experience of Russia’s armed forces will keep serving Moscow well in an era of frequent conventional wars. A divided, resource-scarce world also magnifies the leverage that Russia’s vast natural endowments give it. Russia is a supplier of oil, natural gas, coal, wheat, fertilizers, uranium, critical metals, diamonds, and other commodities. It regularly plays the role of dealmaker, especially now that supply, not price, is the priority. Europe, for instance, may be weaning itself off Russian fossil fuels, but China’s reliance on those supplies helps offset the asymmetries in the relationship between Moscow and Beijing. The vulnerability of Middle Eastern supply routes during the Iran war has further strengthened Russia’s hand. Perpetual confrontation with the West does not serve Russia’s long-term development. A fiercely competitive, volatile environment also raises the value of Russia’s centralized economic and political systems. In the West, these are often derided as antiquated, inflexible, and harmful to the country’s development. Yet a strong state has helped Russia maintain social, economic, and political stability despite Western pressure and its losses in Ukraine. In an era of heightened polarization, Russia’s centralized, personalized decision-making carries clear advantages over the liberal alternative. Putin governs with little opposition, few divisions within the establishment, and scant pushback from the media, and he can pursue the kind of long-term strategic planning that unpredictable election cycles in the West rule out. The United States, meanwhile, is a divided political mess, presided over by a mercurial president and a dysfunctional Congress. Trump seems not only to respect Putin but also to envy him and his tight grip on Russia. In Britain and France, prime ministers come and go, none able to sustain public confidence. The European Union survives for now, but it makes decisions with excruciating slowness and, within its member states, faces surging support for populist parties eager to topple the bureaucrats in Brussels. As long as the international system favors rivalry over cooperation, security over prosperity, regionalization over globalization, and sovereignty over interdependence, Russia will remain in the top tier of global politics. It will even hold comparative advantages over countries with far greater commercial, financial, and technological capacities. Its rivals will be constrained by their own democratic gridlock and restless electorates. Russia cannot beat the West outright, but it can hold its own and play for a draw—until, that is, today’s competitive and fragmented order gives way to compromise, de-escalation, and stability. THE COMING CALM History moves in cycles, and the current configuration of the international system could prove fleeting. Globalization could return in a new form, and instability could give way to a long stretch of stable peace. The seemingly endless fighting in the Middle East could finally stop; Washington and Beijing might reach a sustainable trade and geopolitical compromise; the European Union may overcome its existential crisis; and a new UN secretary-general could succeed in reviving principles of multilateralism in global affairs. The reversal of the pendulum could begin as early as the coming midterm elections in the United States, if they result in a major defeat for Trump’s supporters on Capitol Hill. In such a world, some of the foreign policy assets Russia now prizes most would begin to lose their value. The softer forms of power, which Russia has long underrated, would matter more. Heavy investment in strategic and conventional forces, for instance, gives Moscow geopolitical heft, but it does nothing to help Russia plug into emerging high-value global supply chains. Were its domestic market as vast as China’s or India’s, Russia could insulate itself from the risks associated with globalization’s return. But its long-term demographic decline forecloses that option. Exporting its way out of hardship by selling even more hydrocarbons won’t work either, given the likely fall in demand for fossil fuels. Competing for large-scale foreign direct investment would be harder still. It requires high levels of interstate trust and transparency, as well as a stable and user-friendly legal framework. The country’s geography offers some advantage. With the world’s longest Arctic coastline, Russia can command a large share of the High North’s resource reserves and of the new shipping routes that will open as the climate warms. But to capitalize on its position as a transit corridor between East Asia and Western Europe, Russia would need long-term, stable partnerships with not only China but also the EU. Such relationships are hard to imagine now. Finally, without a strong civilian high-tech ecosystem, Russia could find itself far behind the United States and China in technological prowess. For over two decades, Russia’s leadership has been tightening its grip on the private sector. Its highly centralized decision-making has helped the Kremlin mobilize resources quickly and head off political and social developments that threaten the state, but it has also suffocated the entrepreneurial energy the country needs to regain its technological edge and compete in the marketplace of tomorrow. Russia’s innovation infrastructure remains rooted in the twentieth-century Soviet state-centered model. But today’s technological transformations—AI and robotics, clean energy, quantum computing, gene editing—demand new modes of interaction between states and private businesses, from global platforms down to the garage startups that often lead in key breakthroughs. BEYOND THE FORTRESS How Russia fares over the long run will depend on its ability to hedge against and prepare for another change in the world order. Its current “besieged fortress” model treats the international environment as a challenge rather than an opportunity. It can minimize immediate external risks, but it also keeps Russia from making full use of its geography, resources, and human capital. Perpetual confrontation with the United States and Europe does not serve Russia’s long-term development. The West may keep declining in power, but it will remain indispensable to Russia’s external environment—sometimes a problem for Moscow, sometimes part of the solution. Peaceful coexistence, and even limited cooperation, is the better path. Restoring ties with the EU matters most of all. These days, it is easy to forget that its member states were once Moscow’s main economic partners and its chief source of new technology and modern business practices. Given the dismal state of Russian-European relations, even a partial rapprochement will take considerable time. Once the conflict in Ukraine ends, however, the two sides could begin the slow work of repair. It is also in Russia’s own interest to do its part to uphold international legal norms, especially those coming from the United Nations and other global bodies, even when that means making concessions and giving up potential short-term gains. To be sure, a world governed by “might makes right” offers Moscow real opportunities in the short run. But over the long run, it is a dangerous game. The international balance of power is swiftly shifting, and new actors are rising. A strong international legal system—backed by all major powers, including Russia—may prove one of the few safeguards against revisionist temptations. Russia is, to the dismay of its critics, holding strong and proving itself in the current moment. But to sustain that success, it will have to look beyond short-term gains and narrow self-interest. It must be able to withstand upheaval in the international system and rapid technological change. Russia has the resources and wherewithal to determine its own course, but it is clinging too tightly to its preference for stability over change. This is understandable, given the painful memories of the 1990s, when change came as catastrophe, costing millions of Russians not just their jobs and savings but self-respect, belonging, even a reason to live. But that preference can also harden into a refusal to adapt—a calcification that has pushed great powers to the sidelines before.
