item.title: The Other War on Terror
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.83
For years, the United States’ political dysfunction has been attributed to large-scale social and economic changes. Experts point to the failures of globalization, rising inequality, reduced social mobility, or the long aftermath of the “China shock” more than two decades ago to explain today’s extreme polarization, collapsing trust in institutions, democratic erosion, immigration backlash, and struggling middle class. Yet there is another widely overlooked factor that is equally central to understanding the United States’ current predicament: the war on terror. Typically, when policymakers and analysts speak of the global war on terror—the defining fact of international affairs for two decades—they discuss the damage done to terrorist groups, the plots that have been thwarted, the rise and fall of jihadi ideology, the many intelligence failures, and, perhaps above all, the two forever wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. These are the scorecards of contemporary counterterrorism. But left out of this framing are the profound effects of this vast war on terror on domestic politics and society. The human statistics alone tell an appalling story: more than 7,000 U.S. troops were killed in action, 53,000 were wounded, and well over 30,000 took their own lives—a staggering number. According to Brown University’s Costs of War Project, these conflicts added $8 trillion to the U.S. national debt, with trillions more projected in the future for veterans’ health care, including for the half million GIs with traumatic brain injuries and posttraumatic stress disorder. Yet even these numbers fail to show the myriad ways in which two decades of war transformed the United States. For years, the fixation on Islamist terror shaped a culture drenched in fear, as voices from politics, the media, civil society, and a swelling counterterrorism-industrial complex insisted that the country faced an existential threat. Amid this climate, the government was given broad new powers to root out and prosecute potential jihadi activity wherever it might be, and the widespread assumption that there might be another terrorist attack began to reshape American society itself. Rather than bringing the country together behind a shared—and narrowly defined—enemy, however, the result has been a dramatic decline in social cohesion. It has contributed to the demise of political bipartisanship, already weakened in previous decades. At the same time, the war on terror fueled an alarming rise in xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment and discredited the country’s political and foreign policy elites. Above all has been the uncontrolled expansion of executive power. This impetus did not begin with the war on terror; generations of American leaders and scholars have sought to increase presidential power, drawing up mechanisms that could sideline civil liberties and intertwine military and police activities. But after 9/11, these contingencies were used to give the executive branch sweeping new authority in the name of domestic security. And today, an authoritarian president is using these powers to target his political enemies. The United States, then, is overdue for a reckoning with the political legacy of the war on terror. THE POWER OF NIGHTMARES Anxiety about extended war has preoccupied American officials throughout U.S. history. In the first years after the country’s independence, James Madison, who would become the country’s fourth president, observed that “no nation can preserve its freedom in the midst of continual war.” More than a century and a half later, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower sounded the alarm about “the acquisition of unwarranted influence” by what he famously called “the military-industrial complex.” As Eisenhower forewarned, “The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.” For many of the decades since, much of that apprehension has been focused on the concentration of power in government and in the broader machinery of war. Yet during the war on terror, parts of society mobilized in parallel with the state and sought to cast a much wider net against a class of perceived enemies. Terrorist acts are typically carried out by secret actors operating within a country’s borders, and 9/11 was the ultimate case in point. The attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon—the first on U.S. soil since World War II—were carried out by foreign nationals inside the country. They were motivated by the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s particular brand of jihadi ideology, which held that major attacks on the U.S. homeland would lead Washington to withdraw support for the apostate rulers of the Muslim world. These themes—which also carried notions of proportional revenge for the number of Muslims previously killed by the United States—and the attacks themselves gave license to Islamophobes throughout American society, including in the political world and policy establishment. The most influential came from the evangelical churches: to their huge audiences, leading televangelists such as Franklin Graham, John Hagee, and Robert Jeffress described Islam as “satanic” and a “heresy from the pit of hell” and its followers as a cult of pedophiles. President George W. Bush sought to tamp down the hatred by insisting that the war on terror was not a war against Islam. But for all his protestations, many saw the war on terror as a crusade—a word that Bush himself used early on until he was told how poorly that played in the Islamic world. His message was further belied by such government actions as the detention of at least 1,200 Muslim men—many of whom were held on immigration charges but treated as high-security risks—and the severe curtailment of Muslim civil liberties by the FBI and other law enforcement in the name of addressing the terrorist threat. The fact that the 9/11 hijackers had been sustained by an efficient Muslim support network within the United States no doubt contributed to these measures, as did reasonable concerns about the potential for online radicalization. Trump blurs the lines between Islamophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment. In the decades since, the persistence of fear-mongering and the growth of anti-Muslim sentiment and hate crimes has been hard to miss. When the Obama administration sought to transfer foreign detainees captured in the war on terror from Guantánamo to facilities in the United States, Republicans depicted them as superhuman terrorists that no U.S. prison could safely secure. The plan was nixed. In 2014, when it was revealed that a jihadi’s laptop found in an Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Idlib, Syria, contained some basic information on bioweapons, members of the flourishing counterterrorism commentariat claimed that terrorists planned to cull the African Ebola virus from victims’ corpses and spray it widely in American urban centers. Candidates for high office found the terrorist threat to be the gift that never ceased giving. Political scientists at Dartmouth, where both of us have taught, recall hearing former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016, tell elderly women in a remote New Hampshire village that jihadis might take them hostage in their homes if they didn’t vote for the tough-on-terror candidate. Claims such as these were contradicted by the actual state of the threat. By 2016, it had been several years since U.S. Navy SEALS had killed bin Laden, and al-Qaeda had not managed a second attack against the United States in 15 years. The few, ostensibly Islamist-related attacks that had happened on U.S. soil were mostly lone-wolf actions, in the sense that they were not deployed and directed by al-Qaeda operatives based outside the United States. Instead, they were radicalized in place through exposure to news reporting, online propaganda, preaching, and the fellowship of like-minded individuals. (A partial exception was the 2009 Fort Hood massacre, carried out by a U.S. army major, who had corresponded with Anwar al-Awlaki, the American cleric with links to al-Qaeda who was later killed by the United States in Yemen.) In 2014, ISIS captured global attention with its claim to a caliphate and insurgency in Iraq and Syria, and it was better than al-Qaeda at recruiting followers in Europe and North America. This group carried out or claimed responsibility for bloody attacks in Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, and Spain. Several of these were devastating mass casualty attacks, but none were in the league of 9/11. Notably, ISIS’s rise in the vacuum created by the U.S. toppling of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was a result, not a cause, of the war on terror. The lack of attacks was not simply luck. Throughout these decades, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement professionals—operating far from the overheated rhetoric of the era—dealt methodically and capably with the terrorist threat. During this period, government agencies achieved a level of integration that had improved dramatically since pre-9/11 days. Foreign intelligence services and civil authorities were tightly coordinated in the effort, making it possible to know who was attempting to cross the United States’ borders. Indeed, by the time al-Qaeda struck the United States again—a 2019 shooting at a Florida naval base that killed three and injured eight—the group was a shadow of its former self. As ISIS made clear, the fading of al-Qaeda did not usher in an age of Aquarius. Yet according to solid longitudinal polling, the degree to which Americans prioritized terrorism no longer reflected quotidian reality. The unanswered and perhaps unanswerable question emerging from this period is whether the relative security Americans enjoyed in the decades after 9/11 owed more to intelligence and law enforcement and domestic security measures than to the progress of the expeditionary wars and targeted killings that were meant to root out the problem at its presumed source. Nonetheless, the question remains a vital one for those who are responsible for anticipating terrorism threats and constructing both defensive and offensive approaches to them. FOREVER WAR TO CIVIL WAR In hindsight, 2016 marked a decisive hinge point in the war on terror, when the primary question shifted from faraway military conflicts to allegedly dangerous new threats at home—and not only those from Islamists. The United States had plenty of experience with nativism before 9/11. But a decade and a half of fear-mongering produced something entirely new. Perhaps nowhere was the legacy more pernicious than in the fusing of terrorist fears with broader anti-immigration sentiment. As numerous postmortems for the 2016 presidential election made clear, stoking anti-Muslim sentiment helped mobilize the Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump’s base, even though economic concerns won him that close election. On the campaign trail and then in office, Trump continually blurred the lines between Islamophobia and broader anti-immigrant sentiment. One day he decried murderers, criminals, and rapists coming across the southern border; the next, he asserted that the migrant flows were cover for jihadis. Perhaps the perfect symbol of Trump’s fusion of the threat of terrorism with the challenge of illegal immigration was his repeated warnings in 2018 about a migrant caravan making its way from Central America to the U.S.-Mexican border—a caravan he claimed had “unknown Middle Easterners in it.” To be fair, the U.S. intelligence community was concerned that jihadis were exploiting chaotic conditions at the border to infiltrate the United States, but the fractured nature of interagency databases made this hard to know. In his effort to appear tougher than any competitor, Trump called for bringing back waterboarding and some unspecified technique that was “a helluva lot worse than waterboarding.” Speaking of ISIS operatives, he also said he would “take out their families.” Still more striking, candidate Trump managed to radiate Islamophobia even as he decried the post-9/11 forever wars, stymieing his Republican rivals and his eventual Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. In a way, this marked a decisive shift in the war on terror toward the American homeland. One of the two candidates for president, one of the country’s foremost politicians, was expressly lumping together a sizable American ethnic minority with external enemies. Even when the subtext of previous policy suggested suspicion of American Muslims, federal leaders never expressed explicit hostility. Trump did. Once elected, he implemented a Muslim travel ban, which he introduced just a week into his term and reformulated repeatedly until the Supreme Court finally approved it 18 months later. He also created a permissive structure for xenophobes and racists, spurring a dramatic increase in hate crimes with victims from minority groups of all kinds and accelerating the disuniting of the United States. In his second term, Trump has gone much further. In 2025, the administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 against alleged members of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang, described them as an invading force, and sent detainees to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center. The Supreme Court required adequate notice to permit habeas challenges, but removals had already begun. In Florida, the government opened a remote Everglades detention compound called “Alligator Alcatraz” that might usefully be thought of as Guantánamo transplanted to U.S. soil, with its geographic isolation and removal from the domain of law. The facility shuttered after a year, but only for reasons of expense; it cost over a billion dollars per year to run. And by then, the administration was making an even more direct connection with the war on terror, as some immigrant detainees were now sent to Guantánamo itself. The Pentagon also became involved, with active-duty personnel providing logistical and operational support for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) detention mission. In other words, institutions created for external war, border enforcement, and domestic policing have now become components of a punitive system against immigrants who may not even have a criminal record. As a practical matter, it became a test bed for the detention of political prisoners, or, as Trump described them, “enemies of the people.” The Trump administration is not alone in using Islamophobia to drive an anti-immigrant agenda. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, for instance, has long been famous for railing against illegal immigration. But as The New York Times put it in August, citing Republican consultants, “Islam has replaced the border as a major concern” for voters. To date, Texas officials have blocked a real estate development that includes a mosque and threatened to withhold state funding from airports that provide washing stations for Muslim prayer, among other steps. Meanwhile, Republican politicians across the country have denounced the electoral successes of Muslim politicians, including Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Some have even suggested that these officials either are not American citizens or should lose their citizenship. Trump has remarked that “jihadists are being elected all over the place.” COUNTERTERRORISM-INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX The sociologist Charles Tilly’s maxim that “war makes the state; the state makes war” applies not just to early modern state formation but also to how the United States’ counterterrorism efforts led to a dramatic augmentation of state powers. The war on terror propelled the United States to collect and combine information, including on its own citizens; classify individuals it considered dangerous; combine both active and reserve component military units for the purposes of population control and law enforcement; and use coercive power under a variety of emergency authorities. It also reinforced an “us against them” conception of public life in which political disagreement could be recast as disloyalty and whole minority groups treated as presumptively suspect. The perception of an enduring terrorist threat increased support for coercive policies, even among Americans otherwise resistant to authoritarian appeals. Of course, the United States faced security threats before 9/11. Yet whereas the Cold War security state depended on accurate intelligence on adversaries’ military forces and key assets, counterterrorism is focused not on large formations or fixed installations but on locating individuals hidden within large populations, both at home and in foreign societies. Defending against al-Qaeda required officials to identify suspicious people, trace money and travel, map personal networks, and act before an attack occurred. After the shock of the 9/11 attacks, Washington developed an information-sharing network that crossed the foreign and domestic divide and could search customs, immigration, intelligence, and regular law enforcement records. Joint Terrorism Task Forces set up by the FBI and state and city fusion centers created by DHS implemented this model in parallel at the local level. Their missions soon exceeded terrorism to encompass other facets of public safety. In time, national security institutions were routinely vacuuming up ordinary police information, and local law enforcement officers were combing through federal intelligence. The structure was built for finding needles in haystacks. Once built, it could search for needles of all sorts. Such capabilities made it easy to expand political control and executive power, should an elected leader choose to use them for these purposes. Top government officials could identify not only suspects but also their associations, movements, communications, and supporters, making these tools convenient for targeting individuals and groups, both real and invented, and stigmatized communities. Commercial platforms increased their reach. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)—which was founded in response to September 11—has contracted with the American software company Palantir for ImmigrationOS, a system intended to assist in the selection and apprehension of deportation targets. Artificial intelligence, and its inherent scalability, has accelerated the process by eliminating the main bottleneck to comprehensive surveillance: scarce manpower. The logic was visible during the 2020 protests in Portland, Oregon, when DHS officers monitored social media, accessed travel and immigration records, and assembled dossiers on protesters and journalists. Unidentified armed federal officers used unmarked rental vehicles to detain people and took some to holding cells in the federal courthouse without explaining what agency held them or why. The federal government’s evolution since 9/11 is reflected not just in its activities and capabilities. Its sheer mass has grown, as well. Since ICE was created in 2003, its annual budget has risen from $3.3 billion to almost $29 billion; in the same period, its corps of armed officers has grown from 3,000 to 22,000. Meanwhile, police forces across the country have transformed from lightly armed constabularies to small-scale armies. Before 9/11, the Defense Department had transferred only $27 million in hardware to local police forces. Since the attacks, the number has climbed to more than $1.6 billion. In numerous jurisdictions, police can now respond to demonstrations with mine-proof armored vehicles, camouflage, body armor, and large-caliber weaponry. The government’s target set has also expanded. In 2025, the White House issued National Security Memorandum 7, which, among other things, designated antifa—a mostly made up, decentralized, left-wing political movement opposed to white supremacy and (per its name) fascism—as a domestic terrorist organization, a status not formally recognized in the law. The memorandum directed Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate organized political violence carried out by those who belong to this supposed network. The offenses were “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity . . . extremism on migration, race, and gender . . . hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality.” The crimes to be investigated by the task forces largely related to protected speech. A subsequent counterterrorism strategy document in May 2026 referred specifically to the “politically motivated killings of Christians and conservatives.” The document treats hostility to Christianity as one of the diagnostic markers for identifying organized political violence, alongside anticapitalism and anti-Americanism. The Trump administration has also used counterterrorism precedents to justify the widespread use of lethal force. Beginning in 2025, the administration labeled suspected drug traffickers as narcoterrorists, giving it legal cover to use military strikes against boats and land sites in Latin America. By August 2026, its operations had killed hundreds of people, often without public evidence to establish a crime or even the basic identities of those targeted. Attacks against Iran in May 2026, meanwhile, killed much of the upper echelon of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Different legal authorities were invoked, but as with the purported drug dealers, the White House used classifications and military practices from the war-on-terror era to justify and conduct its operations. Although Israel’s preemptive and retaliatory reliance on targeted killings has drawn much attention, this mode of warfare characterized the American war on terror very nearly from its outset, including the arming of drones for this purpose; the first armed Predator flew in October 2001. During the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign within the United States, four Americans were killed and three wounded with the same impunity as the 526 targeted attacks conducted outside war zones from 2009 to 2016 during the latter phase of the war on terror. The war on terror’s focus on dangerous individuals, in other words, supplied a template that is now being applied to suspected criminals, foreign officials, heads of government, migrants, and protesters. Domestic military deployment has followed a parallel track. In 2002, Washington established U.S. Northern Command to direct homeland defense and support civil authorities. In 2025, the army created Western Hemisphere Command by combining Forces Command, Army North, and Army South under one four-star headquarters responsible for readiness, homeland defense, and operations across the Americas. Neither change erased statutory barriers to domestic military law enforcement. But both reduced the organizational distance between military forces prepared for overseas combat and missions close to home. Since June 2025, the administration has deployed National Guard personnel or active-duty Marines to six American cities. It has also assigned active-duty personnel to support ICE processing and detention facilities. These steps did not formally merge the military and DHS, but they created recurring joint operations through which domestic coercive missions could expand. Meanwhile, Trump is politicizing the armed forces, basing appointments and promotions on partisan loyalty and degrading or simply ignoring long-standing professional norms. These changes will presumably weaken the institutional barriers to the military’s political use, which concerns the missions the president assigned to military personnel, as in Los Angeles, where National Guard troops and Marines accompanied federal immigration operations. A federal district court found that troops had been systematically directed to perform law enforcement functions, including patrols and traffic control, in violation of the Posse Comitatus Act, and the administration ultimately halted these operations. But Trump has declared that they will resume on a larger scale. The homeland, he thinks, is an excellent place for U.S. armed forces to conduct battles. “We should use some of these dangerous cities as training grounds for our military,” Trump said in September 2025. “We’re under invasion from within. No different than a foreign enemy but more difficult in many ways because they don’t wear uniforms.” Urban opposition has been placed within a vocabulary of war. WHERE DOES IT END? War has not only changed the tenor of American life and enabled a vast expansion of executive power. It has also had a radicalizing effect on parts of the population, including war veterans—a phenomenon that bears echoes of the Freikorps, the groups of disbanded soldiers in Weimar Germany who, once given policing powers against the “Bolshevik” threat, quickly became a lethal paramilitary force. In her history of the white power movement, the scholar Kathleen Belew has shown how a segment of Vietnam veterans joined civilians in building a narrative of betrayal, transferring military skills and organizational forms into paramilitary politics to be redirected against enemies at home. The 1992 Ruby Ridge confrontation and the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing came from that milieu. Today, a recurrence of that pattern can be seen among veterans of Afghanistan and Iraq. Groups such as the Oath Keepers and the Three Percenters recruit current and former military personnel and police officers. Its members used military formations during the January 6 attack, and the founder of the Oath Keepers was convicted of seditious conspiracy. Of these, all had their cases dismissed, were pardoned, or had their sentences commuted by Trump. How dangerous these groups still might be is poorly understood: the Trump administration has banned contact between scholars and military personnel except in the framework of professional military education, so there is no up-to-date survey data or qualitative information on attitudes within the military about political matters. Publicly available government reporting on militias has also dried up. Given that such groups have had practical and rhetorical support from the administration in power, the threat of more violence cannot be discounted. Of course, the war on terror also had an immense role in shaping the international environment that the United States contends with today. Iran is a more capable opponent because the war in Iraq converted Hussein’s Sunni regime into one subject to Iranian influence and helped facilitate an Iranian-backed network (the “Axis of Resistance”) across the region. Islamophobia helped spur the rise of populist right-wing parties in Europe, alongside the migration crisis caused by Syria’s civil war and ISIS’s territorial gains in Syria and Iraq. In Egypt and other Arab countries, authoritarian regimes have consolidated control and gained U.S. support by arguing that they are holding the line against terrorists. And as many as 500,000 foreign civilians were killed or died as a result of the war on terror—a history that has left its own grim legacy abroad. The war on terror created a far more powerful government. In the 25 years since the 9/11 attacks, the commemorations have tended to follow a predictable pattern: recollections of the awful events of that day, the reading of names, the lighting of candles. Beyond the now ritual agreement that Iraq was a huge mistake and that Afghanistan was the neglected theater, the consequences of the United States’ reaction to those attacks—and how it has remade the country—remain surprisingly unexamined. It is well past time to give those consequences much closer attention. The 9/11 attacks accelerated the transformation of U.S. political discord from a disagreement between competing ideological coalitions into a conflict between mutually threatening social identities. Islamophobia was both an early expression of that transformation and an important mechanism through which Americans learned to define internal enemies. Over the following quarter century, this mechanism migrated from Muslims to immigrants, racial protesters, cultural minorities, and, ultimately, partisan opponents themselves. Indeed, the most important domestic political legacy of the war on terror may be that the category “terrorist” gradually shifted from the realm of political violence to a model for thinking about political opponents. Meanwhile, the war on terror created a far more powerful government. After 9/11, the United States built a state optimized for identifying threats before they materialized, relying on ubiquitous surveillance, integrated databases, watch lists, preventive policing, militarized border enforcement, expansive secrecy, remote coercive power, broad emergency authority, and a sorcerer’s apprentice national security bureaucracy. President George W. Bush constructed much of this architecture. But even as he constrained parts of it, President Barack Obama embraced much of what he inherited. Congress repeatedly ratified or declined to dismantle it. Presidential self-restraint became the independent variable in the calculation of democracy’s fate. This posed an obvious latent danger. Institutions created on the assumption that presidents would distinguish genuine national security threats from political enemies were safe only as long as presidents continued to make that distinction. When Trump entered the presidency in January 2017 with an unprecedented vision of executive power that he justified through inflammatory threat rhetoric, he could draw on a highly developed set of tools. The war on terror did not create American authoritarianism, but it certainly reduced the startup costs of an authoritarian presidency. item.title: Avoiding the Next Famine
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.58
In a world of great-power standoffs, climatic tipping points, and technological arms races, global hunger may not seem like a particularly significant problem. Yet last year, a total of 2.1 billion people, or more than a quarter of the planet’s population, experienced food insecurity—meaning they either ran out of food over the course of a year or were forced to reduce the quality or quantity of their diet. Over 260 million faced acute food insecurity, meaning their lives or livelihoods were in immediate danger because they could not get enough to eat. Almost a quarter of all children under the age of five were permanently stunted because of malnourishment and will likely reach lower levels of education, earn less over the course of their lives, and live with more chronic health challenges than properly fed kids. And these startling figures do not reflect the food crises that could be unleashed this year by rising energy and fertilizer prices, decreases in grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, and an intensifying El Niño weather pattern. Food insecurity is terrible in and of itself. But it also has disastrous political consequences. It inhibits economic growth, heightens the risk of violent conflict, and destabilizes governments. These problems, in turn, create trouble for the whole world. That means countries that are not overwhelmed by food insecurity still have strong, self-interested reasons to tackle it—the United States included. In fact, a U.S.-led effort to address hunger would do more than create a healthier and more stable planet. Given the waning goodwill toward the United States, Washington needs an agenda through which it can rebuild global confidence in its leadership and demonstrate the value of international cooperation. Addressing global food security could be at the center of such a plan. Different parts of the world, after all, may have different geopolitical ambitions. But almost no government—northern or southern, democratic or autocratic—wants to see so many people go hungry. There may be no better way to rebuild confidence in the liberal world order and in the United States as a committed member of it than for Washington to address this challenge. FOOD, GLORIOUS FOOD It is difficult to overstate just how intertwined food security is with global development, state security, and even international competition. Malnutrition leads to reduced educational attainment, compromised human capital, and lost productivity, costing the world economy $3.5 trillion a year in forgone economic growth and in added health-care costs. Food price spikes can also exacerbate grievances and lead to riots that destabilize governments; anger over hunger, for example, set the conditions for the Arab Spring protests. In rural areas, food insecurity helps armed groups recruit soldiers and causes disputes over scarce land and water resources. And it causes people to migrate to wealthier states. These reasons are, by themselves, enough for Washington to helm a global campaign to reduce hunger. But so should the fact that leading on global food security means helping shape the future of the world’s entire agricultural system—something China is on a path to do. In 2019, Beijing invested significant capital in securing leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, a role with substantial influence over how governments work together on food-related issues. It is also quickly developing other ways to lead the world on matters of food security. China spends double what the United States spends on public agricultural research and development, and its output of agricultural patents and scientific publications has skyrocketed while U.S. output has stagnated. Thankfully for American officials, the United States is still well positioned to lead the world when it comes to food security. The United States is among the world’s largest agricultural exporters. It was instrumental in founding the UN architecture dedicated to food security, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program. And for much of these institutions’ history, Washington has been their largest donor. In fact, for decades, the United States’ international development agenda was the most ambitious in the world, and it was backed by a willing public. Washington retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. The country still has such a public: in early 2026 polling, a strong majority said that the United States should be a moral leader in the world. But a strong majority didn’t believe it was. Perhaps this is because the United States has been walking away from this legacy and this opportunity to lead. In mid-2025, for example, Congress clawed back nearly $8 billion in foreign assistance funds. The United States is now a reluctant international donor and a surly member of key international organizations. Washington, however, still retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. In addition to increasing foreign assistance, it can leverage trade policies, public investment in innovation, and even its impressive data collection systems. Washington, however, will also need to work multilaterally. And to build credibility, it should advance a practical and achievable agenda with clear benefits for all. One overarching goal for collective action should be increasing predictability wherever possible. The global food system is afflicted by uncertainty across many domains—weather, supply chains, labor, trade, and beyond. This wreaks havoc on policymaking, markets, and livelihoods. Being able to better understand these trends and know what tools will be available to manage them could thus do much to shore up food networks and prepare for disasters. Washington should, for example, work with partners to strengthen the world’s fractured early warning systems and the data that enables them. Early warning of shocks to the food system—such as extreme weather, supply disruptions, economic turbulence—buys critical time for preparation and response. The United States should also spearhead the transition of international emergency food assistance funding away from voluntary, ad hoc contributions to preplanned, multiyear commitments. It should simultaneously encourage more donors to contribute in amounts commensurate with their abilities, starting with itself. Food security is one of the few issues that can bring the whole world together. Solving food emergencies requires more than just additional funding. The United States also needs to work to strengthen international norms that protect access to food during conflict. That means making sure humanitarian groups can get into conflict zones, protecting agricultural infrastructure from attacks, and prohibiting the use of starvation as a weapon of war. These concepts have a long-standing basis in international law, but the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine have demonstrated they need reinforcement. Washington should advance these norms through resolutions and interventions in the UN Security Council and General Assembly and use diplomacy to try to get violators to change their behavior. Food security diplomacy, however, must extend beyond conflict zones. The United States should forge a broad global commitment to avoid unilateral, reactionary policies to agricultural shocks—such as when a grain exporter suddenly bans external shipments in response to price spikes, leaving international buyers in the lurch. Such policies may be politically attractive for governments that want to show citizens they will keep costs down. But they leave other states worse off and often don’t even work at home. Instead, the United States should promote more international financing options that maintain the flow of traded agricultural commodities during periods of price volatility and that fast-track funding to countries facing shocks. Finally, the United States should lead a collective action campaign aimed at protecting agricultural systems from a particularly pernicious challenge: agricultural pests and diseases. Pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of global crop production each year, pushing down rural incomes, driving up consumer prices, and wasting natural resources. The existing international surveillance and response systems for these ailments are limited in scope. But Washington can build global support for more comprehensive ones. MORE WITH LESS The world certainly needs better ways of managing food crisis and risk. But it also needs to foster sustainable agricultural productivity growth—or the ability to produce more food with fewer inputs. Such growth is particularly important where populations are rising, as most food consumed is produced domestically. Only certain food commodities can be easily traded across long distances, so international commerce cannot fully solve food and nutritional supply challenges. The most important step countries can collectively take is to promote innovation. To encourage that process, U.S. officials should start by focusing on international agricultural research centers, such as the World Vegetable Center in Taiwan and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico (both of which the United States helped found). These facilities have long been an engine for progress in productivity, food security, and natural resource management, particularly in the developing world. For example, over the last few decades, international centers have developed flood-tolerant rice and drought-tolerant corn that have prevented crop failure for millions of poorer smallholder farmers. In fact, according to studies by a variety of economists, research undertaken by these centers offers an impressive return on investment—for every dollar spent, ten dollars are gained in the form of yield increases, lower production costs, lower consumer prices, and other benefits. But like many institutions, these research centers have suffered from mission creep and bureaucratic accretion. To maximize their effectiveness, the United States should build global support for refocusing their strategy, streamlining their operations, and making new investments in them. The world needs research to keep just ahead of the latest challenges—such as rising temperatures and new strains of old agricultural diseases. But it should also aim higher. Washington thus ought to work with other actors to tackle tough, high-reward problems that have never had the benefit of a truly concerted international effort. This could include, for example, trying to develop high-yielding perennial or nitrogen-fixing grains that would promote healthier landscapes, reduce labor requirements, and need less fertilizer. It might also feature an endeavor to increase photosynthesis efficiency so that plants can produce more from the sunlight they receive. Such inventions would not only change the world, they would also showcase the power of American innovation and deepen Washington’s ties with its partners. But to enable ambitious research, the United States should take steps to reform the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. The agreement was designed to make plant genetic resources, or seeds and tissue, fully and freely available to researchers everywhere. These resources can be used to breed new varieties of crops that are higher yielding, more resilient to climate change, and more nutritious. But the treaty is falling short. Researchers see benefit-sharing provisions as too costly; developing countries see them as offering too little. As a result, fewer researchers seek material that could accelerate innovation, and fewer countries are willing to share it. The United States should thus push everyone to reinterpret the benefit-sharing provisions in a more generous manner. It should also properly fund the Global Crop Diversity Trust’s endowment, which funds the international seed banks that conserve the biological foundation of food crops (particularly since governments, including Washington, are doing an inadequate job of conserving their collections). And if U.S. officials determine that the treaty cannot be saved, they should lead an effort to draft a new one. Lastly, Washington must do whatever it can to make sure that new agricultural and food technologies are quickly adopted. This will require reforms of the international Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is responsible for developing food safety guidelines that protect consumers and facilitate trade. The commission’s guidelines have significant ramifications for technologies that could strengthen global food security, but the body is slow, underfunded, and controversial. The United States should therefore try to enhance its capacity and legitimacy, including by pushing for increased support to the scientific committees that help set Codex standards. REAPING AND SOWING At a time of rising global competition, there are few issues that can bring the whole world together. Food security is one of them. Almost every government knows that hunger is a problem, and almost all of them at least say they want to address it. If the United States can spearhead a strong effort do so, it could bring the planet together under its leadership. That does not mean Washington should instrumentalize food aid or other agricultural endeavors. The United States should not echo its 1970s policies around food power, during which officials boasted of altruism while attempting to exert political strength by alternatively deploying and withholding its grain supply. Instead, the United States must emphasize mutual benefit. It must persuade other actors that it is a constructive and reliable partner. Doing so will strengthen its diplomatic relationships and increase stability around the world—inherently advancing U.S. interests. Rarely do Washington’s strategic imperatives and humanitarian principles align so neatly. It is rarer still for a U.S. foreign policy agenda to clearly reflect what the American people want their country to be: not just strong, but moral. Food security, in other words, is a unique opportunity for the United States. The country cannot afford to waste it. item.title: Why America Can’t Strangle Iran
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.54
For Iran and the United States, August 24 was Groundhog Day. “We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” declared U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime.” It was the same promise he made in April, when he said that the United States was “imposing a financial stranglehold on the Iranian regime” under what the White House called Operation Economic Fury. It was also akin to the May 2018 rollout of the first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” campaign, in which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that Iran would be targeted by the “strongest sanctions in history.” And it sounded like U.S. President Barack Obama’s promise, made in 2012, that the Iranian government was to face “even more crippling sanctions.” The Iranian economy has certainly felt the effects of all the successive restrictions. Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, the country has experienced little growth and high inflation. As a result, Iranian firms have built less infrastructure and adopted fewer new technologies compared with peers in other developing economies. Iranian households, once increasingly affluent, are now at risk of falling below the state’s poverty line. Yet for the better part of a decade, Iran has been able to resist U.S. economic coercion. Until the recent blockade, it used sanctions-evasion techniques to continue oil exports to its key customer, China. Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions, as currency devaluation reduced competition from imports and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting exports. Iran thereby avoided the kind of runaway economic collapse seen in other sanctioned countries, such as Syria and Venezuela. Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy in ways that sanctions alone could not. Numerous U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have targeted critical industrial facilities, including some of Iran’s most important steel and petrochemical plants. The damage sustained during these attacks has led to major production outages for key industrial goods. The general decline in maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the specific disruptions caused by the U.S. naval blockade have not only reduced Iran’s exports; they have also throttled imports of much-needed capital and consumer goods. According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s GDP is set to contract 5.4 percent this year after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months. Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of the summer. The value of the country’s currency has hit a record low of over two million rials to the dollar. But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse, Iran’s leadership remains better able to resist the coercive effects of sanctions than it might appear. The state of the economy is not yet impinging on Iran’s ability to wage war. Stockpiles of various goods remain deep, thanks to years of sanctions experience. And the Iranian state, with its powerful repressive tools, has figured out how to offload much of the economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while making sure its own needs are met. Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself. ANATOMY OF A CRISIS Iranian officials have acknowledged the country’s economic difficulties. “No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we will not endure,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament and a key power broker, on August 21. (Bessent cited this quote as evidence that U.S. economic warfare was having its intended effect.) During a television interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian expressed frustration that some of his fellow political leaders continue to deny that sanctions are harming the country. “Some say sanctions have no effect at all; I really don’t know what to say to those people,” he remarked. The statements from Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian reflect genuine concern about Iran’s economic trajectory. The speaker and the president are understandably worried about deteriorating public opinion, given the inherent connections between general economic welfare and political legitimacy. But U.S. officials should be wary of overinterpreting these statements. Contrary to what it might seem, neither leader is suggesting that the country’s economy is on the brink of collapse. American assessments of the Iranian economy and the success of economic coercion fail to account for the ways in which sanctions have transformed Iran’s political economy, altering the distribution of economic resources in ways that reinforce its existing power structure. The Iranian leaders who are most vocal about the suffering of ordinary people are not worried about the country’s imminent economic collapse; they are dissenting against a political consensus that has long enabled Iranian elites to deliberately push the pressure of sanctions onto ordinary people. Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian are complaining about the social costs of a policy response that has worked largely as intended. Perhaps more important, U.S. assessments of the Iranian economy miss important dynamics. Typically, the effects of sanctions are described in terms of macroeconomic indicators, including rates of growth, inflation, and currency depreciation. But these measures mainly capture price levels: the value of goods and services. They provide, in other words, a financial—not a functional—view of the economy. To take a functional view, one must look at the dynamics at the firm and household level; they reveal why deteriorating figures in the headlines have not led to Iran’s capitulation. Iranian officials pushed the pain of sanctions onto households and firms. The fundamental dilemma for policymakers in any comprehensively sanctioned country is how to respond to balance-of-payments vulnerabilities, such as when a country runs out of the foreign currency it needs to pay for imports. There are, broadly speaking, two approaches. Policymakers can use expansionary monetary policy to fuel investment, restoring the trade surplus through a combination of higher exports and increased domestic production. Alternatively, policymakers can use monetary tightening and austerity measures to suppress import demand, restoring the trade surplus at similar export levels. When faced with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, Russian policymakers took the first approach. They increased fiscal stimulus, driving a rapid expansion in industrial activity and manufacturing employment that created a distinct war economy. This spending was necessary to increase military production, but it also had the effect of dramatically tightening the labor market, raising real wages for ordinary Russians. That, in turn, blunted the initial effects of sanctions-related inflation. This approach eventually reached its limits, and inflation is starting to bite, but the economic strategy allowed Russia to persist in its war aims despite U.S. sanctions pressure. Iranian officials, by contrast, chose the second course of action. When major financial and energy sanctions imposed by the Obama administration first pushed Iran into a recession in 2012, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called for Iran to adopt a “resistance economy,” focusing on domestic capacities to counteract the sanctions pressure. But Iranian economic policymakers never managed to implement a new industrial policy or set up a new welfare system. Instead, they tolerated inflation, effectively pushing the pain of the sanctions away from the government and onto households and firms. They ran austerity budgets and refused to rationalize production or consumption through direct administration, such as by instituting quotas or price controls. The worsening economic crisis led to weakness in the labor market, allowing employers to engage in wage repression and leading to further pressure on household incomes. At first, this may seem like a policy failure. But in reality, Iranian authorities appear perfectly content to see economic activity slow. Doing so, they believe, will give them staying power in their confrontation with the United States. GOOD TIMES, BAD TIMES Microeconomic data reveal the effects of U.S. pressure on economic activity at the firm and household level. A review of Purchasing Managers’ Index data compiled by Iran’s Chamber of Commerce makes clear how the country’s economic crisis has intensified. Between 2019 and 2023, Iran’s overall economy was in contraction for two-thirds of the period thanks to Trump’s initial maximum pressure sanctions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and disruptions related to the “Women, Life, Freedom” protests. But throughout this period, Iranian non-oil industries experienced modest growth. At the start of 2023, Iran even began to exit its long recession as the overall economy and the industrial sector grew in tandem. By March 2024, living standards were beginning to rise again, buoyed by a roughly 15 percent increase in real incomes. This recovery was derailed by the April 2024 Israeli airstrikes on Iran. Since then, the economic uncertainty associated with recurring military conflict has triggered a prolonged decline in industrial activity, pushing Iran into an even deeper recession. Industrial firms have reported deteriorating conditions for eight consecutive months. But that does not mean these firms are insolvent. Over the last two decades, Iranian companies have developed a practice of maintaining large inventories. This practice allows firms to mitigate the effects of sanctions on supply chains and helps shore balance sheets in a high-inflation environment in which cash loses its value but goods do not. According to filings made by companies listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange, the average “days inventory outstanding” level among Iranian industries is around three months. In sensitive sectors such as electrical machinery, which has been heavily targeted by U.S. restrictions, firms maintain inventories as high as 200 days. These large inventories have been a source of significant economic resilience during the war. Iranian supply chains came under strain as ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dwindled. A shift toward overland trade could not compensate for the loss of container traffic through Iran’s southern ports. But with an ample inventory of raw materials, semifinished goods, and finished products, Iranian producers could keep customers supplied—or at least customers with the means to pay. Tehran has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. Firms kept raising prices to protect their margins, passing higher input costs onto consumers. And as the war continued, these higher prices led to demand destruction. Iranian households, embattled by years of persistent inflation, began to consume less. When they did buy, they increasingly relied on consumer credit, including new buy-now-pay-later schemes and informal loans. Even in special categories such as food, Iranian retailers reported diminished sales volume. The sharp drop in household consumption is clear evidence that economic welfare in Iran is declining. It is why Iranian officials have been forced to acknowledge the pain felt by ordinary people. But even so, the government has thus far failed to intervene to control rising prices. Not only have officials failed to introduce price controls—a move that successfully blunted the economic pain associated with the Iran-Iraq War 40 years ago—they have also discussed the elimination of cash transfers and energy subsidies for large portions of the population. In this respect, demand destruction has acted as a form of rationing, providing a structured way for Iranian political and economic elites to push the costs of the war and sanctions onto ordinary people. Although the government continues to face significant fiscal pressure, it has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. With a monthly inflation rate of under ten percent, Iran is still a long way from the kind of hyperinflation—typified by monthly inflation of over 50 percent—that will make the government’s strategy untenable. Meanwhile, reduced economic activity has provided buffers for the real economy. In financial terms, the Iranian economy is in a worse position than at the outset of the war, but in functional terms, inventory levels are unchanged from December 2025, and supply and demand may find a new balance at a lower level of overall economic activity. Iran’s foremost vulnerability to sanctions and the blockade remains its persistent need for imports, which totaled $17 billion in the first five months of this Iranian calendar year beginning in March. That means imports will likely total around $40 billion by the end of the year, down significantly from $58 billion in the previous year and $72 billion in the year before that. The fall in import demand, driven by inflation and currency devaluation, is evidence of a deeper economic crisis. But in the near term, it will help Iranian policymakers forestall a wider economic collapse, possibly for several years. LOW POWER MODE When Bessent evoked the imagery of an “economic D-Day” in his August press conference, he failed to consider who is standing on the other side of his planned invasion. Although it may not seem like it, the success of Iranian authorities in transferring the costs of both sanctions and the war onto ordinary people represents a form of wartime mobilization. Ordinary Iranians may not wish to be mobilized in this way, but they do not have a choice. In a recent social media post, Trump asked, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” But even if ordinary Iranians were to take to the streets again to protest the financial repression they are enduring, they would once again face the brutal violence of the Islamic Republic. With multiple repressive tools at their disposal, many Iranian leaders believe that the country’s population can be made to tolerate more pain, especially if it is necessary to defeat the United States militarily. To prevail in its economic war, the Trump administration will thus need to asphyxiate 25 million households and more than one million firms. But as breathing slows in parts of Iran’s economy, ample oxygen will remain for the country’s elite.
