item.title: The Rise and Fall of Global Jihadism
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.50
Twenty-five years ago, members of the jihadi group al-Qaeda hijacked four American airplanes, flying two of them into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and one into the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Passengers attempted to seize control of the fourth plane, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. The hijackers killed 2,977 people in total—by far the deadliest single terrorist attack in history. To many Americans, the events of September 11, 2001, seemed to come out of nowhere. Few had even heard of al-Qaeda before the attacks. Yet by September 12, the United States had plunged into what President George W. Bush called “a war against terrorism,” a fight that would persist for decades, ensnare multiple jihadi groups, and extend to all corners of the earth. The United States had many setbacks in this war. The ways in which it attempted to prevent another 9/11, or an even larger-scale attack, entailed massive, often inefficient investments as well as troop losses. Some of its efforts, such as the full-scale wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, were brutally destructive. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular, drove a surge in jihadi recruitment. In the years since 2001, various new jihadi groups—some of them connected to al-Qaeda, some opposed to it—have set up shop in the Middle East and across East and West Africa, where they have fueled bloody civil wars, shattered local communities, and launched terrorist attacks both in the region and outside it. But the war on terrorism has not been a complete failure, either. Al-Qaeda itself is devastated. There have been few jihadi attacks on U.S. territory—perhaps the most important measure of success for most American leaders—in the past two and a half decades. According to New America Foundation data, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people in the United States since 2001, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared in the aftermath of 9/11. And although jihadi groups survive, jihadism has lost much of its ideological salience. Consider what has happened since 2023. On October 7, Hamas, a group that al-Qaeda regularly criticized for compromising on theological principles in the pursuit of its political agenda, launched a bloody terrorist attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 people. Israel went on to kill tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, many of them civilians, and conduct other attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank. In 2025, the United States joined Israel in bombing Iran, and in 2026 the United States and Israel launched a full-scale war with the initial objective of regime change in Tehran. The Israeli war in Gaza led to mass protests around the world, and all of these events offered fodder for conspiracy theories about the enemies of Islam plotting against Muslims. Yet in contrast to the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq or the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, they have triggered no jihadi surge. Indeed, the former jihadis who overthrew the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, quickly sought to make nice with states that have long fought terror organizations, including the United States and Saudi Arabia, upon taking power. A quarter century after Osama bin Laden gave the order for the 9/11 attacks, his successors have not built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States and forcing governments to bend to their demands. The sense of historic possibility that once made the jihadi movement so threatening to Western countries has faded. The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost. THE BIRTH OF A MOVEMENT In late 2001, al-Qaeda appeared ascendant. The movement grew out of the armed struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and it attracted Muslim fighters from around the world. Under bin Laden’s leadership, al-Qaeda had many goals, including helping the Taliban secure power in Afghanistan and training its members for terrorist and insurgent campaigns throughout the Muslim world, but ousting the United States from the Middle East was at the top of the list. Other jihadis prioritized fighting governments that they saw as foreign invaders in Chechnya and Kashmir, toppling supposedly apostate Arab regimes, battling Shiite Muslims, or creating a caliphate. The scale of its attack on the United States gave al-Qaeda an aura of momentum and outsize influence within the jihadi movement and beyond. After 9/11, the movement grew in stature, and fighting the United States and its Western allies, which most jihadis had previously considered a relatively low priority, became a more mainstream objective. The fact that the U.S. government would make few distinctions between al-Qaeda-linked groups and jihadis with a more local focus in its subsequent counterterrorism campaign only reinforced that trend. Several factors had made the 2001 attacks possible. Among them were the many shortcomings in Washington’s approach to counterterrorism, including the mistakes identified by the 9/11 Commission, an independent body set up by the U.S. government in 2002, on which I served as a staff member. Those included poor information sharing among U.S. government agencies, a failure to place on watchlists future hijackers who were suspected of links to al-Qaeda and were believed to be traveling to the United States, a lackadaisical effort to find suspected terrorists believed to be in the United States already, and no response to alarming field officer reports that jihadis appeared to be interested in learning how to fly planes. The Islamic State’s overreach was ultimately its undoing. Just as important was al-Qaeda’s own organizing. Most of its leaders were creative, dedicated, and willing to work with other groups, giving the movement a large network from which to recruit the best operatives. Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, from which it could strategize, plot attacks, and coordinate with its international partners without interference. The CIA estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers attended training camps in Afghanistan in the late 1990s, enabling al-Qaeda to build a small army. Recruits from all over the world, but especially the Middle East, learned the basics of insurgent war. The more promising candidates learned advanced counterintelligence and bomb-making techniques. Some of those who received training went to fight alongside the Taliban against the group’s remaining enemies inside Afghanistan, and the Taliban permitted others to leave the country and rejoin local insurgent groups or terrorist cells around the world. Standout recruits among the mass of volunteers were selected for additional training and assigned to high-priority operations. Many of the 9/11 hijackers, for instance, initially went to Afghanistan with the intention to acquire skills and connections before traveling onward to Chechnya to fight alongside Chechen insurgents against Russian security forces. After they were indoctrinated in the camps, al-Qaeda sent them to attack the United States instead. Most governments around the world paid limited attention to this growing danger and did little to prevent members of terrorist organizations from recruiting, generating propaganda, fundraising, and networking on their soil as long as they did not carry out attacks there. Various jihadi leaders and operatives planned operations in Algeria, Bosnia, and elsewhere from London in the 1990s, for example. Even the United States was relatively lax; Ayman al-Zawahiri, who took over al-Qaeda after U.S. forces killed bin Laden in 2011, had come to the country in the 1990s to fundraise. THE TIDE TURNS, EVENTUALLY After 9/11, the United States’ counterterrorism efforts quickly succeeded in dismantling al-Qaeda’s base of operations. As the wreckage of the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers smoldered, the United States commenced military operations in Afghanistan. CIA officers and special operations forces, working with anti-Taliban groups and bolstered by U.S. airpower, quickly overthrew the Taliban. Many al-Qaeda members died in the fight. Those who survived lost their safe haven and, critically, their training camps, and were forced to flee. Most went to Pakistan and Iran and carried on the group’s operations from there; most of al-Qaeda’s most successful post–9/11 attacks, such as the 2005 bombings of London’s transportation system, were orchestrated from Pakistan. But both Islamabad and Tehran were less accommodating hosts than the Taliban were. Neither allowed al-Qaeda to establish new training camps, and Pakistani authorities, in particular, regularly helped the United States arrest and kill the group’s operatives. Without the large-scale training infrastructure that al-Qaeda had set up in Afghanistan, jihadi groups lost much of their ability to mount as sophisticated or distant an attack as 9/11, but they continued to terrorize local populations across the broader Middle East. The United States gave the jihadi cause new energy with its 2003 invasion of Iraq, a war justified in part by the need to confront terrorism. The subsequent U.S. occupation incited anger across the region and fueled the growth of anti-U.S. militant groups in Iraq. The chaos unleashed by the 2011 Arab uprisings gave these and other groups even more room to grow. The eventual outcome was the rise of the so-called Islamic State (or ISIS), which at its height in 2014–15 controlled territory in Iraq and Syria roughly the size of Virginia and home to millions of people. It attracted tens of thousands more recruits from countries in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Other groups, such as al-Shabab, in Somalia, also came to hold territory where they taxed and menaced the population and planned their operations. Yet persistent American pressure on the remaining jihadi havens bore fruit over time. In Iraq and Syria, the United States steadily eroded the Islamic State’s control until the group lost the last of its territory. Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which involved tens of thousands of U.S. forces, Washington deployed small special operations teams while local partners, trained by U.S. forces and backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence, did most of the fighting (and the dying). In other places such as Libya and Somalia, Washington supported the national armies and local militias battling jihadi forces and engaged in whack-a-mole with jihadi leaders. The advent of the armed drone aided this effort, enabling the U.S. military to gather more intelligence and strike more quickly, and with less collateral damage, compared with traditional airpower. Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services helped, as well. Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there—but it allowed Washington and its partners to uncover and unravel much of the global jihadi web, arresting members of al-Qaeda and other groups and disrupting their operations around the world. No less consequential were massive U.S. investments in homeland security. The Department of Homeland Security, created in 2002, was meant to bring together airport security, border protection, and other parts of the national security apparatus that would be involved in preventing terrorist attacks on U.S. territory. Increased spending at airports, on disaster response, and on improved communication between federal, state, and local officials was meant to ensure that information about new threats would be shared quickly, that terrorists would be prevented from entering the country, and that the response to any future attack would be better coordinated. The FBI made counterterrorism a top priority, and it aggressively investigated individuals suspected of terrorist activity. At times it was too aggressive; civil liberties organizations contend that the bureau detained and questioned large numbers of Muslim men and monitored mosques without evidence of wrongdoing. But overall, the effort was effective at preventing attacks. Each measure bolstered the others. Without training camps, would-be terrorists had no place to gain skills and network. Insufficient training could make them more prone to small mistakes that made their fundraising and recruiting efforts more easily detected. More active U.S. and allied security services would be ready to catch them, and then make the intelligence they gathered from those they arrested available to help target overseas networks and havens. The erosion of jihadis’ havens in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere steadily damaged the groups’ credibility and appeal. At the height of the Islamic State’s power, holding territory demonstrated its prowess and attracted followers who wanted to live in a place governed by the group’s version of Islamic law. But when the Islamic State lost territory, its calls for new fighters to come to defend its self-declared caliphate began to ring hollow. Recruitment became much harder. Fewer and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that increasingly looked like it was losing. OWN GOALS It was not only U.S. pressure that brought about the decline of jihadism. The jihadis themselves repeatedly made choices that reduced their appeal. For one, they made too many enemies. Al-Qaeda’s foes included not just the United States but also other supposed foreign occupiers, such as India, Israel, and Russia. Some strands within the broader movement also opposed regimes in Muslim countries that they considered impious, including the governments of Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen. The Islamic State’s list of foes was even longer; it fought most fiercely against Shiites and other non-Sunni Muslims. Declaring so many enemies enabled these groups to attract a wide variety of followers, but it also meant that they diffused their energy. Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal. Even more damning, it ensured that everyone would attack them. Fighting jihadi terrorism was one of the few causes that united countries around the world, and the United States was able to solicit support for its intelligence and military campaigns from foreign governments that disagreed with Washington on many issues but shared an interest in quashing these groups. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience. Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups turned Muslim publics against them by mistreating Muslim civilians. People who might have been sympathetic to their fights against the United States and other foreign powers did not approve of jihadis’ killing of Saudi police and security officials in 2003 and 2004, for instance, or of an al-Qaeda affiliate’s slaughter of both Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006 and 2007. Such killings diminished the jihadis’ influence. In Saudi Arabia, the government, with the broad support of the public, killed or arrested al-Qaeda members, devastating the group’s operations in the country. In Iraq, the faction earned rebukes from clerics who had previously supported global jihad as well as from more mainstream religious leaders. The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing. Its declaration of a caliphate in 2014 was electrifying to many Muslims, coming at a time when the group seemed to be successfully expanding its borders and fighting off enemies. Yet the project created the conditions for the group’s eventual defeat. As bin Laden himself had privately warned another jihadi leader in Yemen years earlier, building a state would give the United States and other countries a place to concentrate their firepower. When the Islamic State declared its caliphate, not only did its territorial control make the group easier to target but its governing also exposed the group’s brutality. Its maximalist claims also made it impossible to work with other jihadis, let alone other countries. By the mid-2020s, the jihadi movement was in no position to capitalize on upheaval in the Middle East. The war in Gaza, the fall of Assad to former jihadis, and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran all supplied the kinds of grievances, images, and narratives that once fueled the movement’s global spread. But with the important exception of Somalia and large parts of West Africa, jihadi groups have not managed a mobilization comparable with the ones after the 2003 Iraq War or during the rise of the Islamic State. At those times, their ideology still had international momentum. Yet after the definitive collapse of the Islamic State’s territorial project, in most places the idea of global jihad lost its former appeal. The past few years might have provided an ideal opportunity to recruit disaffected Muslim youth in Europe and the Middle East, but the jihadis could not seize the moment. THE UNFINISHED FIGHT Despite the decline of jihadism and the relative safety of U.S. territory from attack after 9/11, it is difficult to claim that the United States won its war on terrorism. Neither major war fought under that banner, those in Afghanistan and Iraq, ended well. U.S. forces swiftly removed the Taliban from power in Afghanistan, eliminating the safe haven jihadis had enjoyed, but the campaign turned into a grinding stalemate and then, in 2021, a humiliating defeat when a reconstituted Taliban retook control of the country. The war in Iraq eventually allowed a better government than Saddam Hussein’s dictatorship to emerge, but it also set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State. These and other wars in the region came at a huge human cost, too. The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated that almost a million people, nearly half of them civilians, died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen between 2001 and 2023. The United States lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq, and more than 50,000 were wounded between the two conflicts. Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021. Counterterrorism efforts did not stop jihadism entirely, either. For years, U.S. military campaigns and effective al-Qaeda and Islamic State propaganda amplifying American and allied abuses kept alive the political conditions that enabled the ideology’s spread. And although no jihadi group was able to carry out another operation on the scale of 9/11, the United States and its allies were the target of numerous plots and attacks by individuals who were inspired by jihadi ideology even if they had never met an al-Qaeda or Islamic State member. Many attempted attacks have been foiled thanks to better countermeasures, but the desire to kill Americans and citizens of other countries on jihadi groups’ lists of enemies has not gone away. Efforts by successive U.S. administrations to take on jihadi propaganda directly—including numerous programs aimed at “countering violent extremism”—were not particularly effective at winning the hearts and minds of people who opposed U.S. policy and were disinclined to trust the United States while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars. It will take constant effort to ensure that jihadis cannot rebuild. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however. At their height, jihadi groups proved capable of spectacular violence, forming alliances amid civil wars and even seizing territory. But they failed to translate those achievements into a durable political project or sustained global appeal. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers anything like the same persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or plausible path to political transformation that it did in the first two decades of this century. Jihadis are not flocking to battle Israel or the United States, and the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers. This leaves Washington with tough decisions about how far it should go to fight the jihadi groups that remain active today. Most of them have survived by getting involved in civil wars that have been highly destructive but have erupted in places that are peripheral to U.S. interests, such as Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. There is a risk that jihadi groups could turn their involvement in these wars into opportunities to create new safe havens from which to organize international attacks. But if the United States attacks them directly, it also risks inviting retaliation and getting bogged down in new conflicts. In places such as Somalia and Yemen, Washington’s solution has been to launch drone attacks on jihadi leaders and operatives and provide limited support to regional governments, warlords, and tribal leaders to keep jihadi groups off balance. Yet as long as the governments in these countries remain weak and security assistance fails to move the needle significantly—or if, as the Trump administration has done in many African countries, Washington cuts its aid entirely—jihadi groups will remain active. The United States must accept that jihadism may never truly vanish. For now, U.S. and allied counterterrorism campaigns and jihadis’ poor track record are keeping these groups relatively contained. But it will take continued, constant effort—intelligence cooperation with allies, drone strikes on jihadi operatives, and military training for local partners—to ensure that they cannot start rebuilding in weak states. All of this is best done behind the scenes, denying jihadis easy propaganda victories and limiting the cost to the United States. If Washington can maintain vigilance without overextending itself, it can keep jihadism a manageable danger rather than letting it once again become a defining threat. item.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.08
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished. In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda. Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether. Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased. For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). In the case of core al-Qaeda, although decapitation and military repression played important roles, the group ended primarily through strategic failure—just as bin Laden feared it would. A MOVING TARGET In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, the U.S. campaign should have been focused on destroying the perpetrators. But the United States failed to clearly define the threat. The Authorization for the Use of Military Force that Congress passed on September 14, 2001, did not mention al-Qaeda at all, instead vaguely identifying Washington’s enemies as “those nations, organizations or persons [the president] determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” A few days later, President George W. Bush echoed that framing. “Our war on al-Qaeda begins with al-Qaeda but it does not end there,” he declared. “It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.” With that, the United States declared war on a tactic, one that had shaped political violence in the modern world since anarchist terrorism swept through Europe before World War I. Washington had set itself a task it could never accomplish. Making the enemy “terrorism” meant its efforts would lack clarity and drag on endlessly. What followed was an ill-focused campaign in Afghanistan (which removed the Taliban from power in Kabul but allowed bin Laden and his cronies to escape) and then the war in Iraq, where al-Qaeda had not even operated until an affiliate emerged after the U.S. military occupation had been in place for a year. The invasion of Iraq did more to prolong the life of al-Qaeda than any other single event, drawing fresh recruits from Sunni populations all over the world, and eventually creating the conditions for the emergence of the Islamic State organization. Still, in the 25 years that followed, sometimes almost despite itself, the United States along with its allies did defeat bin Laden’s al-Qaeda—often with inadvertent help from the group itself. An important factor was the May 2011 killing of Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, an event that undermined al-Qaeda’s coherence. U.S. forces stormed bin Laden’s compound, killed him, and then helicoptered his body to an aircraft carrier and buried it at sea, leaving no possibility for a memorial or focal point for his followers. The documents recovered in that raid were just as valuable to U.S. counterterrorism as bin Laden’s death, offering compelling evidence that he had not been centrally directing the group’s operations for some time. His death did not end al-Qaeda, but it was justice served, and it undercut the ability of his fans to rally around him. By September 2011, U.S. officials were claiming that the number of surviving people directly connected to carrying out the 9/11 attacks was no more than a couple of dozen. But instead of declaring victory over the group at that point and moving on, the U.S. drone campaign, which had begun in 2002 under Bush and accelerated in the early Obama administration, expanded its scope and target set. Instead of so-called personality attacks (which target known leaders), the campaign shifted to “signature strikes,” targeting unidentified individuals or groups who fit a particular profile, not just in Afghanistan and Pakistan but also in Somalia and Yemen. The drone campaign degraded al-Qaeda’s ranks and avenged attempted attacks—for example, by eliminating members of al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate who trained and equipped Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the would-be “underwear bomber” who tried to bring down a civilian airliner in 2009. But drone attacks also catalyzed terrorism: according to declassified FBI interviews, the 2013 Boston Marathon bomber, Tamerlan Tsarnaev (likewise inspired by al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate), told a friend that his killing of an eight-year-old in that attack was justified because children in Afghanistan and Pakistan had been killed by U.S. drones. The drone campaign had a strategic impact on U.S. allies: public attitudes in France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom hardened against Washington’s “global war on terrorism.” Drones were tactically important and probably saved lives, but they did not end al-Qaeda. More critical to that success was intelligence and law-enforcement collaboration among U.S. allies, which remains the bedrock of American counterterrorism. New measures to curb terrorist financing, biometric screening and databases, and new ways of sharing intelligence among allies helped Washington monitor threats beyond American shores. In 2006, for example, close cooperation between U.S. and British intelligence services thwarted an al-Qaeda-linked plot to smuggle the explosive TATP in beverage containers and take down U.S.-bound civilian aircraft over the Atlantic. THINGS FALL APART But much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. A key driver was a backlash against terrorist attacks that hurt Muslim civilians and a resulting loss of support among communities al-Qaeda supposedly represented. Bin Laden knew this was a weakness, and his frustration shows in the communications discovered in the Abbottabad compound. A May 2010 letter he wrote to one of his deputies warns, “This is when we lose the perception of the Muslims towards us, which is that we are the ones defending the Muslims and fighting their biggest enemy, the Crusader Zionist alliance…[and instead] killing those that the general public consider Muslims.” Al-Qaeda started building global franchises in 2004, but they typically emerged out of existing organizations, and their operational ties to core al-Qaeda could be hazy. According to bin Laden’s own assessment, rogue affiliates hurt al-Qaeda’s cause more than they helped it, since most victims of their violence were Muslim civilians, whose families and communities then blamed al-Qaeda. According to the Pew Global Attitudes project, between 2003 and 2011, support for bin Laden personally had dropped in Indonesia from 59 percent to 26 percent, in Jordan from 56 percent to 13 percent, and in the Palestinian territories from 72 percent to 34 percent. In Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding, support for him plunged from 46 percent in 2003 to 18 percent in 2010. A decade after 9/11, bin Laden’s dream of a vanguard uniting Muslims had evaporated. Internal divisions also played a role in al-Qaeda’s demise. The most dramatic split was with the Islamic State, or ISIS, which had started out as an al-Qaeda affiliate before rebranding. In 2014, ISIS conquered major parts of Iraq and Syria, drawing some 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries to join its self-declared caliphate. This was a huge challenge to the original group: al-Qaeda had ideas, but ISIS had territory. ISIS’s trajectory reflected the core problem of dealing with affiliates who did not share (or necessarily even grasp) bin Laden’s strategy. In 2005, bin Laden’s chief deputy, Ayman al-Zawahiri, wrote to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi—the leader of what was then known as al-Qaeda in Iraq and would eventually become ISIS—advising him to stop killing Shiite civilians and beheading hostages in grotesque videos. “Among the things which the feelings of the Muslim populace who love and support you will never find palatable … are the scenes of slaughtering the hostages,” Zawahiri wrote. “We don’t need this.” Zarqawi ignored him. In 2006, a U.S. airstrike killed Zarqawi. But for the next decade, global jihadism shifted firmly in his direction, and against the comparatively more cautious approach of al-Qaeda. Much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. Even as ISIS swamped al-Qaeda, however, the limits of its approach became clear, vindicating Zawahiri’s warning. The first mistake ISIS made was to gather forces and materiel in a concentrated space, becoming a perfect target for conventional military force. Its second error was to enthusiastically embrace gruesome forms of brutality and sadism, antagonizing virtually everyone who did not belong to the group; by 2016, almost the entire world had united against it. Working with Iraqi, Kurdish, and Syrian forces, a global coalition to defeat ISIS had by 2019 recaptured the territory the group had seized and destroyed the caliphate. But for al-Qaeda, the damage had been done: it had lost its foothold in Iraq and split its recruitment base with a younger, flashier brand. Zawahiri’s response was to decentralize and focus on groups in South Asia and North Africa, such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which primarily sought to overthrow local governments. In July 2022, nearly a year after the American withdrawal from Afghanistan, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed Zawahiri. The muted response to his death confirmed the weakness of core al-Qaeda. Today, the apparent head of al-Qaeda is Said al-Adel, who lives in Iran, a Shiite-majority country where, for a decade after 9/11, he and other al-Qaeda leaders and their families spent years living under a form of house arrest, and where his room to maneuver remains strictly limited. He has not even declared himself the group’s leader, perhaps because he fears assassination—but perhaps because there is, in reality, nothing for him to lead. Although the group could one day reinvent itself or carry out attacks sponsored or abetted by Iran, the al-Qaeda that attacked the United States 25 years ago has ended. The United States sometimes accelerated and sometimes slowed the group’s demise. But ultimately, al-Qaeda failed. item.title: Jamaica’s Reparations Push
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.24
Jamaica’s Reparations Push The country is asking the U.K. to consider compensation for the harms of slavery. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Jamaica petitions the United Kingdom for slavery reparations, Argentina renews its claims to the Falkland Islands, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio tours South America. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Jamaica petitions the United Kingdom for slavery reparations, Argentina renews its claims to the Falkland Islands, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio tours South America. Redressing the ‘Gravest Crime’ Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s minister of culture, gender, entertainment, and sport, traveled to London this week to file what the island called a first-of-its-kind petition to King Charles III. The petition asks the highest court of appeal for Commonwealth countries to issue a decision on whether the British trafficking of enslaved Africans to Jamaica from the 17th to 19th centuries was unlawful—and whether the United Kingdom owes financial reparations. The petition made no specific monetary claim, though a lawmaker from Jamaica’s ruling party previously estimated that the U.K. owes Jamaicans around $10 billion. The Jamaican government has the right to lodge such a demand because it is a member of the Commonwealth, itself a vestige of the colonial era. Charles is still Jamaica’s head of state. Jamaica’s petition is backed by the rest of the Caribbean Community, or Caricom. Caribbean countries have played a leading role in the growing global movement for reparations. Since 2013, a Caribbean reparations panel has been refining its list of financial and symbolic demands to redress the harms of slavery. In March, Caribbean nations backed a successful United Nations General Assembly resolution deeming the trafficking of enslaved Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity” and calling for reparations payments. Argentina, Israel, and the United States voted against the resolution, while the U.K. and European Union countries abstained. Then, in June, Caribbean leaders including Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley attended a conference in Ghana that demanded a formal apology for slavery. They also asked for reparations measures, such as debt relief, from countries involved in the slave trade. Jamaica’s reparations push is nonpartisan. The country’s conservative prime minister, Andrew Holness, who has otherwise taken a center-right stance on economic matters and worked closely with the International Monetary Fund, last year called the petition to the British crown a “watershed moment for Caricom and the broader global movement for reparatory justice.” Grange’s trip coincided with the anniversary of the Zong slave ship’s departure from West Africa to Jamaica in 1781. During that journey, the ship’s captain ordered enslaved Africans to be thrown overboard and later tried to claim insurance money for lost cargo. British law viewed enslaved Africans as property for centuries. When Parliament abolished slavery in the British Empire in 1833, the government borrowed funds equivalent to 40 percent of its treasury income to compensate slaveowners for their property losses. The formerly enslaved were never compensated for their stolen wages. Seeking reparations is part of an effort “to rewrite our history from the standpoint of the hunted, and not from the standpoint of the hunter,” St. Lucia’s reparations envoy, Earl Bousquet, told the Miami Herald. He described a push to break free from “mental slavery,” a nod to the words of Jamaica’s Bob Marley. Despite the growing international campaign for reparations, few governments or organizations have agreed to pay them. French President Emmanuel Macron made headlines in May by saying the matter should be addressed but provided no details as to how. In 2022, the Netherlands announced a $230 million fund to address the legacy of slavery, while the Church of England has pledged to set up a $135 million reparations fund. In response to Jamaica’s legal filing this week, a spokesperson for Buckingham Palace said it was working with the Jamaican government to ensure the petition was successfully lodged. But a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. “does not and will not pay reparations.” If the U.K. court draws a similar conclusion, some observers believe that Jamaica could respond by severing its formal ties to the British crown, as Barbados did in 2021. Holness’s government introduced a bill to do so in 2024, but it has not yet advanced in the legislature. Upcoming Events Saturday, Sept. 12, to Sunday, Sept. 13: Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira attends the BRICS leaders’ summit in New Delhi in place of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Tuesday, Sept. 15: The U.S. House of Representatives holds a hearing on policy toward Nicaragua. What We’re Following Education checkup. This year’s PISA scores are out. The test measures 15-year-olds’ proficiency in math, reading, and science in countries around the world. Many Latin American countries saw their scores decline in line with a global trend. The education and skills director of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, which administers the test, told the Wall Street Journal that poor policies regulating smartphone and artificial intelligence use might be to blame. But the PISA exams also showed that certain uses of AI in education could be promising. In El Salvador, an additional school-level PISA test compared schools that were implementing reforms—including an AI tutoring program—with those that were not. Schools with the program had significantly better results. The World Bank, which is backing the reforms, praised them as a case to continue studying. Falklands flare-up. Argentine President Javier Milei gave a formal address last week claiming that the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory, should be administered by Argentina. It was an effort to rally nationalist sentiment as his popularity wanes and households feel the economic pinch from Milei’s austerity program. This week, Argentina announced that it would impose sanctions on energy companies drilling for oil near the Falklands, which it calls the Malvinas. Milei said the companies could be blocked from operating at Argentina’s Vaca Muerta oil and gas fields. Unlike in the past, both U.S. President Donald Trump and a far-right Israeli cabinet member have signaled that they might support Argentina’s position, likely thanks to Milei’s alignment with Trump and new a U.K. ban on trade with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Most countries across the global south support it as well. One major remaining obstacle, Antonio De Loera-Brust wrote in Foreign Policy in July, is the desire of the islanders themselves, who prefer being ruled by Britain. Pan-American humor. Chilean standup comedian Fabrizio Copano went on the pan-Latin America El Hilo podcast last week to discuss the role of humor in turbulent political times. Born in Chile’s capital, Santiago, Copano now lives in New York and does shows in both English and Spanish across the Western Hemisphere. “I think humor is still lucky enough to be able to make people laugh even when they don’t agree with what’s being said,” he said. Copano often tells his U.S. viewers that “Latin Americans come from the future”—they know what it’s like to get by when politics is dysfunctional, part of which includes being able to laugh. Copano naturalized as a U.S. citizen last year. He said in a recent comedy special that he really felt he was becoming American after taking his car in for a repair. The technician gushed about how much he loved Chile. He was thrilled. But the technician added that his favorite part about Chile was former dictator Augusto Pinochet. Copano thought for a moment about taking a stand for Chilean democracy, but then the man said he would give Copano a discount. He swallowed his dissent and accepted the lower price. Question of the Week FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal In Focus: Rubio’s South America Tour U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru this week. All three countries now have right-wing presidents who have pledged close security cooperation with the United States and joined Trump’s Shield of the Americas anti-gang initiative. Washinton provided few details about the grouping when it was launched in March, though members vowed to support a militarized approach to fighting drug trafficking. Rubio’s trip delivered more specifics about the nature of that cooperation. In Ecuador, Rubio said there had been a recent shift in the U.S. approach to targeting alleged drug boats in the region. The United States was now carrying out more joint operations with South American countries in their own territorial waters, rather than unilateral U.S. strikes in international waters, he said. Rubio did not clarify when the change occurred. But in the last two weeks, the U.S. military has announced a series of interdictions off Ecuador’s coast of boats that allegedly served as refueling stations for drug runs. The crews were removed before the boats were bombed, in contrast with the previous norm. But the deadly strikes are continuing. The U.S. military announced one on Wednesday in the Caribbean but did not specify whether it took place in international waters. That brings the number of people that the United States has killed in its yearlong campaign to at least 230. Rubio said the United States would soon provide Ecuador with naval interceptor vessels; U.S. troops have already begun anti-gang land operations in the country. Speaking in Barranquilla, Colombia, Rubio said the country had not requested U.S. boots on the ground but rather equipment and training aid, which the United States planned to provide. item.title: The United States Must Prepare for More Than One Russian Future
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.10
The United States Must Prepare for More Than One Russian Future Managing the Ukraine conflict is just the beginning of negotiations. After more than half a year of drift in U.S.-brokered talks, Washington recently sent envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Washington is right to resume talks, but U.S. diplomacy toward Russia remains too episodic. Witkoff and Kushner’s meetings in Moscow and Kyiv produced no breakthrough, and there is little sign that either side has moved appreciably on the core issues. High-level shuttle diplomacy can reopen doors, but it cannot substitute for sustained official channels and the institutional capacity to use them. After more than half a year of drift in U.S.-brokered talks, Washington recently sent envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Washington is right to resume talks, but U.S. diplomacy toward Russia remains too episodic. Witkoff and Kushner’s meetings in Moscow and Kyiv produced no breakthrough, and there is little sign that either side has moved appreciably on the core issues. High-level shuttle diplomacy can reopen doors, but it cannot substitute for sustained official channels and the institutional capacity to use them. Still, whether or not this latest push leads to anything, the war in Ukraine will eventually end at a negotiating table. What happens on the battlefield will shape the terms of any cease-fire or settlement, but it will not substitute for one. Russians and Ukrainians will ultimately have to reach terms that each can live with, and any durable agreement will almost certainly require deep and sustained U.S. involvement. Vital as it is, managing the Ukraine conflict will be the beginning, not the end of U.S.-Russia negotiations. Moscow and Washington will also have to deal with each other on nuclear risk and strategic stability, outer space, the Arctic, pandemics, and responding to disasters, among many other issues. None of this requires a return to “normal” relations, much less trust or friendship. It requires something more basic: the ability to conduct difficult business with a difficult counterpart when important U.S. interests demand it. The problem is that after more than a decade of increasing pressure and isolation, especially since 2014, the United States has lost much of that ability. There are good reasons for imposing costs on Russia. Moscow’s aggression against Ukraine, interference in Western political systems, repression at home, and increasingly hostile posture abroad demanded consequences. But policies have second-order effects. One of them has been the hollowing out of the human and institutional infrastructure by which the United States once managed sustained engagement with Moscow. This matters because the Russians are tough negotiators. Generations of U.S. officials and experts who have sat across the table from Russian counterparts came away impressed by their discipline and preparation. Ambassador Rose Gottemoeller, who negotiated the New START treaty, described her Russian counterparts in an interview with me as “crack negotiators,” extremely well trained, fluent in the negotiating process, technically capable, and often possessing an advantage in language skills. Russian negotiators also tend to pay very close attention to Americans. That reflects a persistent asymmetry in the relationship. For Moscow, Washington has often been among the very highest foreign-policy priorities. For Washington, Russia has had to compete with China, the Middle East, Europe, terrorism, trade, domestic politics, and everything else occupying a superpower’s attention. In the post-Soviet period, veteran U.S. officials recalled Russian counterparts studying U.S. politics, personalities, and institutional dynamics in extraordinary detail, while Americans sometimes arrived with less experienced teams and far less bandwidth. That does not mean that Russians possess some secret national negotiating code. They make mistakes, misread opponents, overreach, and frequently fail to achieve their goals. And of course, individuals vary as much as Americans or anyone else. But they almost always come to the table with a strong sense of representing a great power, deep institutional memory, careful preparation, and acute sensitivity to questions of status and respect. At the same time, the decision-making process to which they are subject can be rigid and highly centralized. An experienced American negotiator learns to distinguish between an opponent who will not move and a counterpart who simply cannot. That kind of judgment is learned through experience, not briefing books. The United States has had to learn this lesson before. Direct U.S.-Soviet engagement began expanding even during some of the hardest years of the Cold War. The 1958 Lacy-Zarubin agreement opened exchanges in science, medicine, education, culture, and other fields. By the 1970s, Washington and Moscow had built formal channels not only for arms control but also for cooperation on health, agriculture, environmental protection, science, and technology. These programs existed even amid the depths of the Cold War precisely because they were seen by both sides as important tools for managing conflict. By the late 1980s, the dialogue led by U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz and Soviet Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze had become even more structured. Its famous “four-part” agenda covered nuclear arms control, regional conflicts from Afghanistan to Central America, bilateral issues such as trade and energy, and human rights questions including Soviet Jewish emigration. The point was not necessarily to seek agreement on this wide array of topics. Rather, it was to ensure that there was a process capable of carrying disagreement without risking potentially dangerous showdowns or requiring every issue to be elevated to the presidential level. Post-Cold War administrations kept relearning the same lesson. The bilateral commission led by U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin created cabinet-level working relationships across space, energy, health, science, and other fields. The George W. Bush administration tried a smaller strategic dialogue intended to identify problems, clear bureaucratic logjams, and elevate issues requiring presidential attention. Finally, a commission created by U.S. President Barack Obama and Russian President Dmitry Medvedev combined senior political oversight with more than a dozen working groups. Each model had flaws. Some became too bureaucratic. Others depended too heavily on personalities. But the fact that Washington and Moscow kept constructing this kind of institutional machinery for negotiations shows that sooner or later, they found that they needed it. Washington has now spent years dismantling that machinery and, even more consequentially, losing the experience required to use it. The generation of U.S. officials formed by repeated negotiations with Soviet and Russian counterparts is leaving government. Behind them is a cohort of highly capable U.S. experts, but many have spent the most important years of their careers in an environment defined by sanctions, diplomatic expulsions, and mutual isolation. Knowing Russia through study, even having spent time in countries bordering Russia, is not the same thing as knowing Russians and how to negotiate with them across a table, repeatedly, over months or years. American diplomat George F. Kennan himself made this leap in 1933. After two years studying Russian language, history, and culture in Berlin and another two at the U.S. diplomatic listening post in Riga, Latvia, Kennan joined Ambassador William Bullitt’s small team charged with establishing the first U.S. embassy in Moscow since the Bolshevik Revolution. For all that preparation, Kennan later recalled in his memoirs that he had never actually been to Moscow and that it was only then that his education as a Russia expert became an education in dealing with Russians. None of this requires waiting for a political thaw. There are practical steps that the United States can take now, even in the midst of a deep freeze in official relations. First, the United States should capture the knowledge that remains. Veteran diplomats, arms control negotiators, military officers, and other officials who spent years dealing directly with Soviet and Russian counterparts should be systematically debriefed, through oral histories, case studies, and after-action reviews focused not only on what was negotiated, but also how. Second, Washington should train for negotiations before it needs them. The State Department, Defense Department, and National Security Council can conduct realistic simulations involving Russian institutions, personalities, negotiating practices, and chains of authority, drawing heavily on officials with Russian language and regional expertise. Third, U.S. officials should rebuild their map of the other side. Allied governments, track 1.5 dialogues, academic exchanges, and the limited contacts that remain can help identify the next generation of Russian officials, understand how Russian institutions have changed during the war years, and distinguish formal titles from actual influence and authority. Finally, Washington should determine which official channels must remain functional even if the confrontation were to get worse. Crisis communications, nuclear risk reduction, and military deconfliction cannot be improvised after something has gone wrong. Those channels should be maintained and, where possible, exercised. Nor should U.S. officials wait for a sudden political opening in Moscow to discover who can pick up the phone, who has authority on the other side, or which parts of the U.S. government know how to turn a presidential directive into sustained negotiations. Washington should prepare for more than one Russian future. Putin could remain in power, and confrontation with the West could persist or intensify. A settlement in Ukraine could create only a narrow opening for limited engagement. Or a leadership transition, internal upheaval, or other black swan event could produce a much larger and less predictable opportunity. These scenarios would demand very different policies. All would demand negotiating capacity. Preparing for that day now is no concession. Diplomacy is never a reward for good behavior, and negotiation is not normalization. It is an instrument of national power. For the past decade, the United States and its allies have invested heavily in their ability to impose costs on Russia, constrain its options, and deter further aggression. Those capabilities remain necessary. But leverage has value only if the United States also knows how to turn it into outcomes. Sooner or later, U.S. officials will again sit across the table from Russian counterparts. Preparing them to succeed should begin now. Matthew Rojansky is president and CEO of the U.S. Russia Foundation and a visiting scholar at Dartmouth College. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Who Wears the BRICS Crown?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.38
Who Wears the BRICS Crown? India and China compete to shape the bloc’s agenda moving forward. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at what to expect at this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, the legacy of 9/11 a quarter century later, and the Houthis’ lightning offensive on the Red Sea coast. Vying for Influence In a world long dictated by U.S. hegemony, who leads the other side? That is the issue defining this weekend’s BRICS summit, as the leaders of Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and other member countries gather in New Delhi to discuss what a counterweight to Washington’s influence should look like. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at what to expect at this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, the legacy of 9/11 a quarter century later, and the Houthis’ lightning offensive on the Red Sea coast. Vying for Influence In a world long dictated by U.S. hegemony, who leads the other side? That is the issue defining this weekend’s BRICS summit, as the leaders of Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and other member countries gather in New Delhi to discuss what a counterweight to Washington’s influence should look like. BRICS was established in 2009 as a direct response to the U.S. dollar’s dominance in international trade as well as Washington’s leverage over the United Nations and what was then the G-8. But the bloc’s ability to make significant headway has long been stymied by internal dissent, especially between India and China. This weekend, New Delhi and Beijing will jockey for dominance over the bloc’s agenda going forward. On Friday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi set the mood for the two-day summit by agreeing to strengthen his country’s special relationship with Russia. According to India’s foreign ministry, Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as vowed to continue negotiations over defense and energy issues. India is the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. New Delhi previously vowed to increase bilateral trade with Moscow from nearly $70 billion in 2025 to $100 billion by 2030, despite repeated U.S. threats against countries that trade with the Kremlin or continue to purchase Russian crude. At the same time, New Delhi has managed to maintain its close ties with Washington in a way that most other BRICS governments, including Beijing, have failed to do. Meanwhile, experts say Chinese President Xi Jinping will aim to push his own agenda during what will be his first visit to India in seven years. Over the weekend, he is expected to hold a sidelines conversation with Modi to discuss a long-running border dispute, opportunities for greater Chinese investment, and their shared roles in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. He is also likely to push India on its massive trade deficit with China, as Beijing is New Delhi’s biggest business partner. But dissent between the bloc’s two wealthiest nations will not be the group’s only schism. The U.S.-Iran war—and Tehran’s attacks on U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf—has also increased tensions among the group’s members. During a BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in May, also held in India, the bloc failed to come to a consensus on how to address the conflict. Then in August, the United Arab Emirates (a BRICS member) suspended all trade with fellow member Iran over its continued attacks on Emirati soil. Despite the theme of this year’s summit being “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability,” BRICS nations may find it difficult to achieve the level of collaboration needed to craft a cohesive message amid growing internal disunity. Today’s Most Read - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - How Could Iran Happen? An Autopsy. by Ariane Tabatabai and Julia Curlee What We’re Following Remembering 9/11. Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the United States, considered the deadliest foreign assault on U.S. soil in history. Seven moments of silence were observed at a memorial ceremony in New York City to mark the times when hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania. The silences also recognized when both New York City buildings collapsed as well as all those who later died from cancer or other illnesses from inhaling toxic dust in the attack’s aftermath. More than 2,900 people were killed, including hundreds of first responders, on Sept. 11, 2001, and at least 9,500 others have died from 9/11-related diseases. “Twenty-five years on, it’s still hard to grasp the significance of 9/11 because it remains a moving target,” FP columnist Michael Hirsh argues. The attacks led then-U.S. President George W. Bush to launch a “war against all those who seek to export terror and a war against those governments that support or shelter them.” A quarter of a century later, the United States continues to contend with the legacy of that global war on terrorism, including the fallout of its disastrous withdrawal from Afghanistan and the continued fight against Iran and its proxy groups. “We will never, ever forget,” U.S. President Donald Trump said at a separate ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice.” He thanked active service members fighting in the Middle East for “working right now to ensure the world’s No. 1 sponsor of terror—the Islamic Republic of Iran—will never, ever have a nuclear weapon.” Major Houthi victory. Houthi rebels in Yemen seized control of several strategic Red Sea islands and port cities on Friday, solidifying their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait. “Everything that was under our control on the western coast has fallen,” said a military official with the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed Yemeni government. That includes the Houthis’ takeover of Perim Island, the Greater and Lesser Hanish Islands, and Zuqar Island as well as the coastal Yemeni town of Dhubab. Fighting between Houthi and Saudi-led forces has escalated in recent weeks, as the Iranian proxy group has carried out a lightning offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast. On Thursday, Houthi rebels claimed the critical port city of Mokha in a major blow to Riyadh’s military efforts. However, Friday’s victories may be even more detrimental to Saudi Arabia’s ambitions in the country, as it gives Iran leverage over another crucial waterway. Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz has severely hampered the global economy, disrupting supply chains, raising oil prices, and injecting greater insecurity into the region. With the Bab el-Mandeb now under the thumb of an Iranian ally, experts expect these problems to only grow. Still, Tehran confirmed on Friday that it would meet with Iraqi and Gulf state representatives in Oman on Monday to resume negotiations on reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic. Eroding democracy. A Hong Kong court sentenced three local activists to prison on Friday in a case seen as symbolic of the city’s declining democratic freedoms since Beijing imposed its strict national security law in 2020. Lee Cheuk-yan, Chow Hang-tung, and Albert Ho were convicted this year of inciting subversion under that law by organizing annual vigils to commemorate China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. All three individuals were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China and have been in custody for years. “Even when the defendants believed their agenda of ‘end one-party dictatorship’ might breach the constitution and the national security law, they acted recalcitrantly after the national security law took effect and vigorously promoted their cause,” the three-judge panel wrote. Both Lee and Chow had pleaded not guilty; they were given a seven-year and seven-year, three-month sentence, respectively. Their loved ones confirmed on Friday that they planned to appeal. Ho, however, pleaded guilty and was therefore given a reduced five-year, two-month prison term. What in the World? The far-right Alternative for Germany party won a state election on Sunday but fell short of the majority needed to form a government without a coalition. If the party succeeds in coalition- building, it would be the first far-right party to lead a German state since when? A. The fall of the Berlin Wall B. World War II C. The Soviet consolidation of East Germany D. The Weimar Republic Odds and Ends When road rage threatens to get the best of you, Kenyan street performers are ready to help. Acrobats, jugglers, and other entertainers have recently taken on Nairobi’s busy roads by performing for motorists stuck in the capital’s notorious traffic jams. “There are no opportunities for us that we can go to,” street acrobat Jackson Okoth told The Associated Press, referring to Kenya’s high unemployment rate. “So we like it when we are here because it keeps us busy and it keeps us fit also.” And the Answer Is… B. World War II The rise of the far right in Germany signals the end of German postwar democracy as we know it, John Kampfner argues. To take the rest of FP’s weekly international news quiz, click here, or sign up to be alerted when a new one is published. item.title: How Congress Empowered Presidential War-Making After 9/11
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.30
How Congress Empowered Presidential War-Making After 9/11 Its effects continue to shape national security policy today. Americans live in a perpetual state of war. Although Congress has not formally declared war since 1942, U.S. presidents have repeatedly deployed troops overseas based on United Nations resolutions, congressional authorizations, or their own executive power—as President Donald Trump has in Iran. But the power that presidents possess in matters of national security is not the product of an inevitable expansion of the executive authority. Congress builds the imperial presidency one step at a time. At key moments in U.S. history and in response to international threats, Congress has made deliberate decisions that have resulted in presidents being allowed to deploy troops and assert executive power over civil liberties. Americans live in a perpetual state of war. Although Congress has not formally declared war since 1942, U.S. presidents have repeatedly deployed troops overseas based on United Nations resolutions, congressional authorizations, or their own executive power—as President Donald Trump has in Iran. But the power that presidents possess in matters of national security is not the product of an inevitable expansion of the executive authority. Congress builds the imperial presidency one step at a time. At key moments in U.S. history and in response to international threats, Congress has made deliberate decisions that have resulted in presidents being allowed to deploy troops and assert executive power over civil liberties. One of the most consequential moments came in the aftermath of the horrific attacks of 9/11. Just days after Americans suffered the deadliest-ever attack on U.S. soil, Congress passed the Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) with bipartisan support. The measure placed the nation on a permanent wartime footing, greatly expanding the range of actions a president could take without seeking additional congressional approval. Although some skeptics succeeded in narrowing the scope of the authority granted by the legislation, it remained so broad that its effects continued to shape national security policy today. Understanding the decisions Congress made in the weeks following 9/11 is as important as commemorating the tragedy itself. Those decisions shaped how the nation would respond to terrorist threats, the constitutional safeguards Congress was willing to sacrifice in the name of security, and the damaging consequences for the balance of power that resulted from elected officials’ efforts to protect the country. The 9/11 attacks devasted the nation. The destruction wrought by al Qaeda killed Americans, destroyed the World Trade Center and portions of the Pentagon, and left the country deeply traumatized. Americans had grown accustomed to the protections afforded by two vast oceans. Although it had been a long time since the nation could consider itself truly insulated from global affairs—and although the advent of nuclear weapons during World War II meant that everyone, everywhere, was potentially vulnerable to attack—a devastating strike against the homeland on the scale of 9/11 was profoundly shocking. Bush responded aggressively. In contrast to President Bill Clinton, whose administration had addressed the 1993 World Trade Center bombing primarily through domestic law enforcement and the criminal justice system, the Bush administration treated the events of 9/11 as an act of war. Of all the decisions made in the weeks following 9/11, few were as consequential as the passage of the AUMF. Determined not to waste time, Bush worked with congressional leaders to draft legislation authorizing the administration to respond to the attacks with military force. Bush sought the broadest possible language, language that would make President Lyndon Johnson’s 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution—which granted him authority to use force in Vietnam—seem modest by comparison. The president wanted a bill that would empower him not only to pursue those responsible for the attacks but also to “deter and pre-empt any future acts of terrorism or aggression against the United States,” as his administration’s draft text put it. That would’ be roughly the equivalent of Congress granting him a blank check for war. In the aftermath of 9/11, Democrats were fearful of looking weak on national security (a charge that the GOP had used effectively since the 1960s) and Republicans were eager to support their president; even so, they pressed the administration to accept slightly narrower language. The final legislation authorized the use of force against those who “planned, authorized, committed, or aided” these specific attacks, as well as any country that had given refuge to terrorists. Despite the slightly narrower language, the authority Congress granted was sweeping. The limits were largely illusory, as the legislation did not specify against whom force could be used, where the force could be employed, and when the authorization would end. The structure of the legislation also freed the president from the constraints that Congress had imposed with the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which had sought to limit presidential power to use military force after the quagmire in Vietnam. Although the War Powers Resolution had always been flawed, the AUMF rendered it nearly irrelevant in matters that could be justified as part of the response to 9/11. On Sept. 14, the day that Bush made a historic visit to Ground Zero with first responders, the Senate passed the AUMF by a vote of 98-0. The sole dissent in the House of Representatives was California Democrat Barbara Lee. (Ten other representatives abstained from voting.) In a blistering speech, she warned that her colleagues were repeating the mistakes of earlier wars—no matter how just—by expanding government power in the name of national security; she said that they were creating a dangerous precedent that would allow future presidents to act overseas with little regard for Congress. Lee pleaded that as the nation was in a “state of mourning,” Congress should “pause, just for a minute and think through the implications of our actions today.” Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain, who helped narrow the language with Massachusetts Democrat John Kerry, acknowledged that he still had concerns given the Gulf of Tonkin precedent. On Sept. 18, Bush signed the bill into law. His Office of Legal Counsel promptly claimed that the president’s power was even more sweeping than the law proclaimed: John Yoo wrote a memo stating that the president still had the power to launch preemptive attacks against potential threats. The congressional authors of the bill were proud of what they had done. Then-Sen. Joe Biden, who helped craft the measure, boasted: “We gave the president all the authority he needed without giving up our constitutional right to decide whether force should be used.” Defending the law, Arizona Republican Sen. Jon Kyl explained, “I’m not for putting a lot of strings on it. Are we going to be able to give the president enough flexibility to act if we put a lot of restrictions in legislation?” The first major use of the law came in October 2001, when the administration started bombing Afghanistan to bring down the Taliban regime that had harbored al Qaeda. Bush also relied on the AUMF to justify the detention of suspected terrorists at Guantánamo Bay, the detention facility in Cuba that administration officials argued lay outside sovereign U.S. territory and was therefore beyond the reach of certain constitutional protections, including the writ of habeas corpus. The administration invoked the AUMF when it established military commissions to try terrorism suspects, rather than go through the legal system. It also authorized expansive and sweeping surveillance programs conducted by the National Security Agency. While Congress voted for a separate authorization to use force in Iraq, Bush cited the 2001 law to justify why troops should be sent to topple Saddam Hussein: “The use of armed force against Iraq is consistent with the United states … continuing to take the necessary actions” against “those nations, organization, or persons who planned, authorized, committed, or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” Congress never rescinded the 2001 AUMF. Presidents of both parties have relied on it to conduct military operations. President Barack Obama, who campaigned against many aspects of the Bush administration’s war on terrorism and criticized the expansive use of executive power, nevertheless depended on the law to authorize drone strikes and special operations in numerous countries, including Yemen and Somalia. He also initially invoked the AUMF to support military action against the Islamic State in 2014, arguing that the group was a successor to al Qaeda. The “existing statutes,” he said, “provide me with the authority” he needed to wage war. Trump and Biden likewise relied on the legislation to support military operations and counterterrorism activities. Attempts to repeal the AUMF have failed. Over time, Lee was no longer alone in her opposition, but Congress nevertheless refused to repeal or significantly curtail the authority it had granted. As a result, even in 2026, presidents continue to wield far broader military powers than they did before 9/11, including in military operations that are only tenuously, if at all, connected to the attacks that the nation suffered 25 years ago. If either party is serious about reining in presidential power, addressing the AUMF would be an important place to start. Repealing or substantially reforming the measure would be a vital step toward restoring some of the authority Congress has ceded and require the current president (and future presidents) to obtain legislative approval before using military force abroad. Although doing so would not fully reverse the erosion of congressional authority that has occurred in recent decades, it would represent a significant step by eliminating a clear and tangible source of power that presidents have long had at their disposal. But Congress will need to restore its own power. In Washington, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi was known to say, nobody gives you power; you have to take it. For too long, Congress has been willing to cede war-making power to the president for a variety of reasons, from partisan loyalty to a desire to avoid blame when military operations go poorly. Whatever the rationale, the imbalance has reached dangerous levels, as became clear when Trump unilaterally committed the country to a costly, months-long operation that has further destabilized the Middle East and potentially strengthened Iran’s economic leverage. Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. His most recent book is The Presidency of Joseph R. Biden Jr.: A First Historical Assessment.
