item.title: A War Reporter’s Antidote to Nihilism
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.79
A War Reporter’s Antidote to Nihilism In a new book, Sally Hayden considers how journalists can puncture the detachment of the privileged. European society was historically divided into a general hierarchy known as the three estates: the clergy, the nobility, and the hoi polloi—that is, everyone else. Working along those lines, the Parliament of the United Kingdom classifies its members in a similar system: the Lords Spiritual, the Lords Temporal, and the Commons. It was during a sitting of the House of Commons that Edmund Burke, a member of Parliament in the late 18th century, apparently identified a new type of estate. “Burke said there were Three Estates in Parliament; but, in the Reporters’ Gallery yonder, there sat a Fourth Estate more important far than they all,” wrote Thomas Carlyle, the 19th century historian, in his book On Heroes, Hero Worship & the Heroic in History. Both he and Burke recognized the strange contradiction experienced by journalists: the necessity of being both part of and separate from the world, of creating impartial accounts of tumultuous events even as they’re living through them—something Sally Hayden understands only too well. European society was historically divided into a general hierarchy known as the three estates: the clergy, the nobility, and the hoi polloi—that is, everyone else. Working along those lines, the Parliament of the United Kingdom classifies its members in a similar system: the Lords Spiritual, the Lords Temporal, and the Commons. It was during a sitting of the House of Commons that Edmund Burke, a member of Parliament in the late 18th century, apparently identified a new type of estate. “Burke said there were Three Estates in Parliament; but, in the Reporters’ Gallery yonder, there sat a Fourth Estate more important far than they all,” wrote Thomas Carlyle, the 19th century historian, in his book On Heroes, Hero Worship & the Heroic in History. Both he and Burke recognized the strange contradiction experienced by journalists: the necessity of being both part of and separate from the world, of creating impartial accounts of tumultuous events even as they’re living through them—something Sally Hayden understands only too well. Hayden, an award-winning Irish journalist and author, has spent her career living out the maxim that good journalism should comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable, often reporting from war zones, disaster sites, and politically unstable regions fraught with violence. Her work has helped the rest of the world understand what’s happening on the ground in real time, and to say that she has risked her life in order to be a voice for the voiceless is not an exaggeration. But she is also keenly aware that the zoomed-out journalistic view, which is necessary for relaying the broad scope of a situation in brief and digestible communiqués, means sacrificing details about the people involved, smoothing out the texture of their lives and folding it into the larger story. Often, only the direst information remains, while the personal—the relationships, the love—is left out. This troubling reality is what led Hayden to write her second book, This Is Also a Love Story: A Reporter’s Search for Goodness in a Cruel World. In it, she looks at crisis situations at a human level, telling stories that show how love—frequently manifesting as bravery, selflessness, and tenacity—shapes these events just as much, if not more so, than cruelty, greed, and abuses of power. That might sound like treacly Hallmark nonsense; in Hayden’s capable hands, however, it’s anything but. This is Also a Love Story is an ambitious book, covering a lot of ground both geographically and thematically. Each chapter considers a different country and is organized around a different aspect of love, such as unlawful queer love in Ghana and the love of chosen families created in Rwanda in the wake of the 1994 genocide. The bulk of the countries featured in the book are in Africa and the Middle East, mapping onto where Hayden’s career has taken her, though she also writes about Ukraine and Japan. In each place, she follows several individuals, offering multiple perspectives on the same theme. Some of the accounts in the book are fleshed-out versions of stories that Hayden worked on several years ago. For example, she writes about time spent in Nigeria in 2016 and 2017 while reporting on atrocities committed by Boko Haram. The subject of this chapter is the fierce love of mothers protecting their children; the least harrowing story is that of a woman who spent months hiding her 12-year-old daughter in a pit, frightening her daughter’s would-be abductors off by rubbing feces on herself. Here, as elsewhere, Hayden’s language is clear and unsparing: The woman “demonstrated how, while pretending to be mentally unwell, she would pull her other daughters close to her,” she writes. “Flies swarmed around her, attracted to the excrement. This was another ploy to save her younger children.” In a few cases, Hayden was able to reconnect with previous interview subjects, such as Fadwa Mahmoud, a Syrian woman whom she first interviewed in 2022, a decade after Mahmoud’s husband and son were disappeared by Bashar al-Assad’s brutal regime; her story is included in a chapter that highlights the horrors of loving a missing person, someone who may no longer be alive but whose death you may never be able to confirm, leaving you forever trapped in a terrible limbo. Hayden witnessed the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 more or less firsthand—once it was clear the rebel forces had prevailed, she was able to quickly travel there from her home in Lebanon—and her reporting highlights the ambivalence the liberation sparked in many people. “Exuberance was accompanied by the sudden unveiling of what had previously been only whispered about, a seeping abhorrence,” Hayden writes, describing the emptying of military prisons in characteristically evocative prose. Syria’s newfound freedom was bittersweet for those whose missing family members were still unaccounted for even after all the political prisoners were freed. Some chapters, on the other hand, are made up of interviews that seem to have been conducted specifically for the book—for example, the one on Ukraine, which focuses on the complications of having a partner who is away fighting on the front lines. The writing in these sections is as excellent as elsewhere in the book, but the stories themselves feel as if they lack the depth of some of the others, perhaps because Hayden has not spent years mulling over and regretting parts of interviews that were left on the cutting room floor. It’s also possible that these chapters feel weaker because they take place outside of the regions from which she typically reports. Still, Hayden for the most part succeeds at knitting all the stories together by finding the common points of humanity across great differences. Speaking of regret, it (or something approximating it) was one of the catalysts for This Is Also a Love Story. “I have often worried that news reporting is dehumanising, reducing people, and the dense complexity of their lives, to basic facts and figures or overly simplistic and reductive headlines,” writes Hayden in the prologue, clearly calling herself to account for her own role in this dehumanization. At the same time, she admits that she feels “damaged by the violence and impunity” that she has witnessed as a journalist, which has led to a “blunting ennui that harden[ed] into cynicism and a sense of futility.” Countering this sentiment seems to have been another animating factor when it came to choosing her subject matter. However Hayden may feel about the toll her career has taken on her, This Is Also a Love Story makes it obvious that her empathy is still intact. She has the journalist’s gift of painting detailed pictures without getting bogged down in an excess of descriptive language. The result is a book where her interview subjects feel fully human, with all of the complications that entails, while the chapters themselves are exactly the right length and depth to be thoughtful and engaging without dragging. Hayden’s focus on love never feels like naiveté or unearned optimism, but rather a call to action. It’s easy for the privileged to engage in a world-weary sort of nihilism, arguing that humanity is terrible and doomed and not worth saving; it’s a way, to put it baldly, for us to talk ourselves into the idea that doing nothing is somehow fine—maybe even laudable. The more difficult truth is that most people are mostly good, and all of us are vulnerable (though some, of course, more than others) to the dangers of war, unrest, and general disaster. But acknowledging this is frightening. It’s much more pleasant to believe that bad things happen to people who might deserve it because of beliefs they hold or choices they have made. Hayden knows all of this, of course; she experiences it near-daily in her line of work. But rather than being didactic about how grim things are, she instead holds up these lovingly rendered portraits of people caring for each other through difficult times, gently encouraging readers to avoid the temptation to “withdraw into solitude” as a way of coping with their fear and discomfort, but rather to meet the world with “empathy and compassion.” After all, she writes, “what is empathy or compassion but love turned towards humanity itself?” The three estates of the realm may no longer be an accurate description of how power, particularly in geopolitics, plays out. But Burke’s idea of a fourth estate—a group that sits outside of the power structure and holds it accountable—feels more necessary than ever as global inequality grows and vulnerable groups are being increasingly left behind. And yet, as Hayden demonstrates, reporting on a crisis with details like the number of dead, wounded, and displaced can only ever be part of creating that accountability; in order to bring about real change, journalists must find a way to puncture the detachment of the privileged. This can only be done by adding humanity to that raw data, infusing it with what Hayden refers to as “the elaborate beauty of other people’s existence, including the loves that drive and bind them.” Fortunately for us, This Is Also a Love Story helps to do just that. Anne Thériault is a writer based in Ontario, Canada, who has contributed to the Walrus, Quill & Quire, Broadview Magazine, the London Review of Books, and many other publications. item.title: What Happens When AI Starts Doing Business with AI?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.59
Summary. As AI agents increasingly interact with one another on commercial platforms, firms need new rules governing what those agents can see, decide, and do. In a controlled AI-to-AI simulation covering In late 2025, Perplexity’s Comet browser began logging into shoppers’ Amazon accounts and buying on their behalf. Amazon treated it as an intruder. It blocked the agent and when Perplexity slipped past the block within a day, Amazon took the dispute to federal court. WeChat drew the line differently. After shutting out ByteDance’s Doubao assistant, which used system-level access to navigate WeChat without permission, Tencent later opened what it describes as an agent-to-agent channel to selected assistants from Huawei, Xiaomi, and others to send messages and place calls. Under this arrangement, an external agent translates a user’s request into a structured instruction and passes it through a Tencent-controlled interface to WeChat, which executes the action inside its own environment. Tencent controls which agents can connect, which functions they can invoke, and what data and execution remain inside WeChat. In other words, one platform shut the door to AI agents outright; the other unlocked it on its own terms.

item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.77
Summary. Today, a single individual enabled by AI can—at very low cost—perform many activities needed to establish a startup quickly and in parallel: generating product ideas, simulating Almost two decades ago, the entrepreneur and author Eric Ries launched a methodology for the “lean startup.” In this approach, a new business could be launched with just capital, a minimum viable product, a team, extensive discussions with potential customers, and a process of repeated pivoting as the startup scaled. The lean startup approach combined Toyota’s lean manufacturing method with Stanford professor Steve Blank’s approaches to customer development. Because founders typically had few resources at their disposal, the lean approach took hold.

A more revealing approach is the curveball: a question that is closely tied to what We’re all taught to ask tough questions. Interviewers are coached to use open-ended prompts to get beyond rehearsed answers. Managers press for specifics when employees speak in generalities. Journalists and negotiators follow up when someone evades the point. The aim is the same: to uncover information the other person may be reluctant to reveal.

item.title: How Industrial Goliaths, Not Davids, Stand to Win the AI Decade
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.69
For the better part of two decades, the story of industrial disruption had a familiar shape. Nimble entrants ran circles around the incumbents, unburdened by legacy portfolios, tangled supply chains, or installed bases measured in decades. The advantage belonged to whoever carried the least. AI is inverting the story. The same weight that slowed large manufacturers—the sprawling product histories, the regulatory scar tissue, the decades of hard-won engineering intellectual property (IP)—is precisely the raw material that makes AI valuable. In discrete manufacturing, the winners of the AI decade will not be the startups with the cleanest slate. They will be the Goliaths who finally turn their bulk into leverage. The Asset No One Can Buy Here is the uncomfortable truth for every well-funded newcomer: The one thing they cannot acquire is history. A general AI model can learn everything on the public internet and still know nothing about how your product is designed, built, changed, and certified. That knowledge lives in the engineering systems established manufacturers have run for years—the requirements, designs, bills of materials, and change history that constitute the essential IP of a business, along with the rules governing who may see it and how it gets approved. That is exactly the context AI needs to reason well: what it is working with, who is allowed to use it, and how similar problems were solved before. Strip that away and even a capable model is reduced to guessing. Owning It Isn’t the Same Thing as Wielding It There is no partial credit here: Either a manufacturer’s product data is connected, governed, and curated or it isn’t. And for most, it isn’t. When a manufacturer’s product data sits fragmented across systems that don’t talk, modeled inconsistently across functions, locked in PDFs and the memories of engineers who may be five years from retirement, that is not a company with a slightly weaker AI position. It is a company with no AI position at all, pointing retrieval-augmented generation at a pile of disconnected documents and calling the output intelligence. Take a routine scenario: A supplier discontinues a component and a replacement has to be qualified. In one company, an engineer spends weeks tracing where that part lives: which assemblies, which configurations, which customer variants, which open orders, and which regulatory filings reference it. In another, an AI agent reaching the live product record through an open standard like the Model Context Protocol returns the full ripple in minutes, flags the two variants where the substitution breaks a compliance requirement, and surfaces a part already qualified for the same purpose. Same change, same models, same ambition. But one company absorbs the cost quietly; the other never pays it. And that is one scenario among dozens that play out every week, such as: - A field failure comes in from a customer. One company reasons across service records, the as-built configuration, and the change history to find the root cause in an afternoon; the other convenes a task force and waits. - A new program goes out to bid. One company knows in hours which existing designs, parts, and lessons it can reuse; the other quotes as if starting from scratch and either overbids or wins work it will lose money on. - An auditor asks for the complete design and approval trail on a shipped product. One company produces it on demand; the other sends people digging through inboxes and shared drives for a week. - A design engineer starts a new part. One company’s AI surfaces the three interchangeable parts already in the catalog; the other creates a fourth and pays to carry it for its entire lifecycle. None of these is a dramatic, board-level crisis. Each is a small, ordinary moment of product work. And that is the point. Here, the math tips toward the giant: the larger the portfolio, the deeper the installed base; the longer the history, the more of these moments occur every day and the more a connected foundation compounds across them. The same scale that was a liability for 20 years becomes the multiplier. On disconnected data, that scale only multiplies the drag. Those returns don’t come on a sliding scale. They belong entirely to the manufacturers whose data is ready to be reasoned over, and not at all to the ones whose data isn’t—a divide decided long before the first model is deployed. A Strategic Decision, Not a Software Purchase Closing the gap is less about buying new software than about making a decision: to own and govern product data as an enterprise asset, not a by-product of engineering. Three things unlock it: - A product data foundation, anchored in the bill of materials, so AI reasons over an authoritative connected model rather than fragments that disagree. - Governed AI, where the same access rules that protect the IP constrain the model to limit what each user may see, keeping the model secure and auditable rather than a novel way to leak secrets. - AI in the workflow, running within the procedures teams already use, from engineering change to configuration to manufacturing planning, rather than hovering above them as a chatbot. The executives who win this decade won’t be those who ran the most AI experiments. They’ll be those who asked the harder question early: Are we turning decades of engineering IP into a structural advantage or letting it depreciate in systems that don’t connect, align, or scale? For 20 years, size was a liability. AI is making size the ultimate advantage—but only for the manufacturers who build the foundation to wield it. The advantage is already theirs. The only question is whether Goliath picks up the stone—before David convinces him he’s too big to fight.
